nodes.name: Smart Truck (AD2 kit)
nodes.description: Forward camera, radar, compute box, driver display and the harness that talks to the vehicle. The biggest single line in the plan and the one the mandate is written for. Forty percent of group revenue from one SKU. That is the concentration to underwrite — also why the portfolio has a demand floor rather than a forecast.

nodes.name: AD0 Smart Mirror
nodes.description: A replacement rear-view mirror with an integrated display, four body cameras and a wiring loom. Fitted in an afternoon — the least sophisticated thing we make, and it ships first. Volume ramp of the portfolio: highest unit count and lowest fitment complexity — scales channel reach that harder products inherit.

nodes.name: Autonomous TaaS
nodes.description: Transport-as-a-Service: contracted autonomous operations — DeepGrid provides the vehicle, stack and driver replacement as a metered service. Highest revenue per unit we sell. Proof that the same silicon running in a kit can run an entire operation.

nodes.name: Chipset OEM B2B
nodes.description: The bare die, in tray or reel, for a customer to place on their own board. No enclosure, no cables, no fitting — silicon and a datasheet. Fifty-four crore at ninety-four percent gross margin — the highest in the portfolio. Every rupee arrives without installation capacity or warranty logistics.

nodes.name: T100 AI Licence
nodes.description: Indian road perception models, toolchain and continuous model updates licensed to third-party compute platforms. Pure software revenue at 94% margin. Converts the IP investment in Indian road models into a recurring stream independent of hardware.

nodes.name: AD1 Indoor L4 Kit
nodes.description: Self-driving retrofit kit for indoor vehicles: sensor head, compute box and drive-by-wire interface. Fitted to forklifts and tugs a site already owns. Where L4 behaviour ships years before it is legal on a public road — the technical proof point for the road roadmap.

nodes.name: A100 Compute Box 4ch PCIe
nodes.description: Four-channel PCIe compute card for multi-camera deployments — industrial inspection, security and infrastructure monitoring. The highest-capacity compute form factor — serves customers who need multi-camera perception without building their own board.

nodes.name: Defence D-HUMR
nodes.description: Defence-grade unmanned ground reconnaissance platform. Hardened compute, encrypted comms and ruggedised sensor suite. Highest price point in the portfolio — opens defence procurement channel and validates ruggedised silicon.

nodes.name: A100 Compute Box 2ch
nodes.description: Dual-channel compute board for stereo vision and dual-camera applications. Mid-tier compute module serving stereo vision applications.

nodes.name: A100 Compute Box 1ch M.2
nodes.description: Single-channel M.2 module — the smallest configuration the part supports. Same die, running less. Entry-level compute module — lowest-cost path to adding DeepGrid perception to an existing product.

nodes.name: Seaport AGV
nodes.description: Autonomous container yard vehicle — 7cm open positioning, 22cm under crane. Moves containers between quay crane and yard block. Second-highest revenue per unit after TaaS — validates the silicon in port infrastructure.

nodes.name: D100 Drone SoC Kit
nodes.description: Aerial inspection and surveillance compute kit — same SoC2 in a drone-optimised form factor. Opens aerial perception as a silicon market — same die, different firmware.

nodes.name: Thermal Camera Pod
nodes.description: LWIR thermal camera sensor module for night and monsoon conditions — the perception layer that cameras alone cannot provide. The perception layer that enables night and monsoon operation — differentiator for the Smart Truck kit.

nodes.name: H100 Driver Monitor
nodes.description: In-cabin driver monitoring unit — drowsiness, distraction and seatbelt detection. Mandate-listed safety function. Highest volume sensor SKU — mandate requires it in every commercial vehicle.

nodes.name: 4D Radar Pod
nodes.description: 4D imaging radar module providing range, velocity, azimuth and elevation — the sensor that camera-only ADAS cannot replace. Radar matters because closing speed is what a braking decision actually turns on — camera alone cannot measure it.

nodes.name: SoC2 (28 nm monolithic SoC)
nodes.description: TSMC 28nm monolithic SoC2. A 57mm² die with six compute domains: A100 neural processing, R100 radar DSP, T100 AI, D100 security, S100 vehicle control and H100 monitoring. 39.3 TOPS is derived architecture arithmetic, not measured silicon performance. Eleven sensor channels have an 8.6 ms fusion design target in a 33.3 ms frame.

chunks.title: Smart Truck (AD2 kit)
chunks.text: Smart Truck (AD2 kit) (Road Autonomy, Systems). Forward camera, radar, compute box, driver display and the harness that talks to the vehicle. The biggest single line in the plan and the one the mandate is written for. Price ₹2,50,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹450 Cr, 39.9% of the plan, gross margin 89%, first revenue FY2027, volume 18,000 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Forty percent of group revenue from one SKU. That is the concentration to underwrite — also why the portfolio has a demand floor rather than a forecast. From sensing to action: Camera and radar watch the forward path and the blind quarters; SoC2 fuses both into one object list carrying range and closing speed; Collision, lane and blind-spot logic decides whether to warn; Driver is warned; where vehicle supports it, brake interface is signalled. Key dependency: AIS-mandate compliance, installation channel capacity, and radar verification milestones.

chunks.title: AD0 Smart Mirror
chunks.text: AD0 Smart Mirror (Road Autonomy, Systems). A replacement rear-view mirror with an integrated display, four body cameras and a wiring loom. Fitted in an afternoon — the least sophisticated thing we make, and it ships first. Price ₹50,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹270 Cr, 23.9% of the plan, gross margin 89%, first revenue FY2027, volume 54,000 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Volume ramp of the portfolio: highest unit count and lowest fitment complexity — scales channel reach that harder products inherit. From sensing to action: Four cameras cover the vehicle's blind quarters; SoC2 stitches the views into one 360° surround image; Proximity and motion logic flags anything entering the danger zone; Driver sees the stitched view and hears a directional alert. Key dependency: Distribution reach and price holding at ₹50k. Runs on current-generation hardware — not gated on the ASIC.

chunks.title: Autonomous TaaS
chunks.text: Autonomous TaaS (Fleet & Mobility, Services). Transport-as-a-Service: contracted autonomous operations — DeepGrid provides the vehicle, stack and driver replacement as a metered service. Price ₹66.00 L. FY2032 revenue projection ₹66 Cr, 5.8% of the plan, gross margin 89%, first revenue FY2028, volume 100 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Highest revenue per unit we sell. Proof that the same silicon running in a kit can run an entire operation. From sensing to action: Route plan set by fleet management system; SoC2 handles full perception and planning stack; Vehicle drives autonomously within geofenced route; Fleet dashboard monitors all units in real time. Key dependency: Regulatory clearance for autonomous operation in controlled corridors.

chunks.title: Chipset OEM B2B
chunks.text: Chipset OEM B2B (Silicon & Compute, Components). The bare die, in tray or reel, for a customer to place on their own board. No enclosure, no cables, no fitting — silicon and a datasheet. Price ₹18,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹54 Cr, 4.8% of the plan, gross margin 94%, first revenue FY2028, volume 30,000 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Fifty-four crore at ninety-four percent gross margin — the highest in the portfolio. Every rupee arrives without installation capacity or warranty logistics. From sensing to action: Customer's own sensors feed their own board; Our die does the perception compute inside their design; Their software decides what to do with the result; Their product ships with our silicon inside it. Key dependency: ASIC tapeout completion and qualification.

chunks.title: T100 AI Licence
chunks.text: T100 AI Licence (Silicon & Compute, Software). Indian road perception models, toolchain and continuous model updates licensed to third-party compute platforms. Price ₹100.00 L. FY2032 revenue projection ₹50 Cr, 4.4% of the plan, gross margin 94%, first revenue FY2029, volume 50 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Pure software revenue at 94% margin. Converts the IP investment in Indian road models into a recurring stream independent of hardware. From sensing to action: Customer integrates perception SDK on their hardware; Models trained on Indian road conditions run inference; Continuous model updates delivered via licence subscription; Customer product ships with DeepGrid perception layer. Key dependency: Maturity of the Indian road perception stack — starts FY29.

chunks.title: AD1 Indoor L4 Kit
chunks.text: AD1 Indoor L4 Kit (Road Autonomy, Systems). Self-driving retrofit kit for indoor vehicles: sensor head, compute box and drive-by-wire interface. Fitted to forklifts and tugs a site already owns. Price ₹1,00,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹42 Cr, 3.7% of the plan, gross margin 89%, first revenue FY2028, volume 4,200 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Where L4 behaviour ships years before it is legal on a public road — the technical proof point for the road roadmap. From sensing to action: Cameras and depth sensing read the aisle, load and people; SoC2 localises the vehicle against a site map it holds onboard; Planner picks a path and a speed for the geofenced route; Drive-by-wire interface issues steer, throttle and brake. Key dependency: Site mapping and commissioning throughput — services capacity rather than product.

chunks.title: A100 Compute Box 4ch PCIe
chunks.text: A100 Compute Box 4ch PCIe (Silicon & Compute, Modules). Four-channel PCIe compute card for multi-camera deployments — industrial inspection, security and infrastructure monitoring. Price ₹3,00,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹36 Cr, 3.2% of the plan, gross margin 89%, first revenue FY2028, volume 1,200 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: The highest-capacity compute form factor — serves customers who need multi-camera perception without building their own board. From sensing to action: Up to four camera feeds enter via PCIe interface; SoC2 runs parallel perception on all four channels; Object lists and alerts output to host system; Customer software consumes structured perception data. Key dependency: ASIC tapeout and PCIe interface validation.

chunks.title: Defence D-HUMR
chunks.text: Defence D-HUMR (Sensors & Robotics, Systems). Defence-grade unmanned ground reconnaissance platform. Hardened compute, encrypted comms and ruggedised sensor suite. Price ₹20,00,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹30 Cr, 2.7% of the plan, gross margin 68%, first revenue FY2027, volume 150 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Highest price point in the portfolio — opens defence procurement channel and validates ruggedised silicon. From sensing to action: Ruggedised camera and thermal sensors scan terrain; SoC2 runs perception with military-grade encryption; Autonomous navigation in GPS-denied environments; Secure data relay to command post. Key dependency: Defence procurement cycle and security clearances.

chunks.title: A100 Compute Box 2ch

FY2032 revenue projection ₹28.8 Cr, 2.5% of the plan, gross margin 89%, first revenue FY2028, volume 1,800 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Mid-tier compute module serving stereo vision applications. From sensing to action: Two camera inputs; Dual-stream perception; Fused output; Host integration. Key dependency: ASIC tapeout.

chunks.title: A100 Compute Box 1ch M.2

FY2032 revenue projection ₹25.5 Cr, 2.3% of the plan, gross margin 89%, first revenue FY2028, volume 3,000 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Entry-level compute module — lowest-cost path to adding DeepGrid perception to an existing product. From sensing to action: One camera in; One perception stream out; Standard M.2 interface; Drop-in to existing enclosure. Key dependency: ASIC tapeout.

chunks.title: Seaport AGV
chunks.text: Seaport AGV (Fleet & Mobility, Systems). Autonomous container yard vehicle — 7cm open positioning, 22cm under crane. Moves containers between quay crane and yard block. Price ₹45,30,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹22.6 Cr, 2.0% of the plan, gross margin 89%, first revenue FY2028, volume 50 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Second-highest revenue per unit after TaaS — validates the silicon in port infrastructure. From sensing to action: GPS-RTK and vision provide centimetre-level localisation; SoC2 plans path through dynamic yard traffic; Autonomous steer/throttle/brake in open and under-crane zones; Yard management system dispatches and monitors fleet. Key dependency: Port authority partnerships and certification.

chunks.title: D100 Drone SoC Kit
chunks.text: D100 Drone SoC Kit (Sensors & Robotics, Modules). Aerial inspection and surveillance compute kit — same SoC2 in a drone-optimised form factor. Price ₹5,00,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹20 Cr, 1.8% of the plan, gross margin 68%, first revenue FY2028, volume 400 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Opens aerial perception as a silicon market — same die, different firmware. From sensing to action: Gimbal camera + thermal sensor; SoC2 runs airborne perception; Object detection and tracking; Telemetry relay to ground station. Key dependency: Drone regulation and form-factor development.

chunks.title: Thermal Camera Pod
chunks.text: Thermal Camera Pod (Sensors & Robotics, Components). LWIR thermal camera sensor module for night and monsoon conditions — the perception layer that cameras alone cannot provide. Price ₹50,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹16 Cr, 1.4% of the plan, gross margin 50%, first revenue FY2027, volume 3,200 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: The perception layer that enables night and monsoon operation — differentiator for the Smart Truck kit. From sensing to action: LWIR sensor captures thermal scene; SoC2 fuses thermal with visible camera; Enhanced detection in low/no visibility; Alert output to vehicle safety system. Key dependency: LWIR sensor sourcing and calibration pipeline.

chunks.title: H100 Driver Monitor
chunks.text: H100 Driver Monitor (Sensors & Robotics, Components). In-cabin driver monitoring unit — drowsiness, distraction and seatbelt detection. Mandate-listed safety function. Price ₹5,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹10 Cr, 0.9% of the plan, gross margin 50%, first revenue FY2027, volume 20,000 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Highest volume sensor SKU — mandate requires it in every commercial vehicle. From sensing to action: IR camera watches driver face; SoC2 runs drowsiness/distraction model; Alert escalation chain triggered; Event log for fleet compliance. Key dependency: Mandate enforcement timeline.

chunks.title: 4D Radar Pod
chunks.text: 4D Radar Pod (Sensors & Robotics, Components). 4D imaging radar module providing range, velocity, azimuth and elevation — the sensor that camera-only ADAS cannot replace. Price ₹25,000. FY2032 revenue projection ₹7.5 Cr, 0.7% of the plan, gross margin 50%, first revenue FY2027, volume 3,000 @ FY32. Role in the portfolio: Radar matters because closing speed is what a braking decision actually turns on — camera alone cannot measure it. From sensing to action: 4D radar scans forward scene; Range + velocity + angle data output; SoC2 fuses radar with camera object list; Closing-speed data enables braking decisions. Key dependency: Radar block verification on the ASIC.

chunks.title: UC-01 AEBS forward-path perception
chunks.text: AEBS forward-path perception. Standard: AIS-162 / IS 11852:2019 · CMVR 96(12). Dates: 1 Jan 2027 new models · 1 Oct 2027 all models. Challenge: Rule 96(12) obliges AEBS plus Vehicle Stability Function on M2/M3/N2/N3. The system must warn at least 1.4 s before it brakes and may not enter the emergency phase before TTC 3.0 s. That budget is a perception problem; the braking is not. What Deepgrid supplies: Detection, classification, tracking and per-target TTC on a documented interface, with confidence and sensor-health state. Actuation, calibration, homologation and warranty stay with the Tier-1. Steps: Forward camera into the module: classify car, truck, bus, two- and three-wheeler, pedestrian and animal from 25 km/h to max design speed, at every load state; Track each target, estimate range-rate, compute per-target TTC and in-path probability; Emit a ranked object list with per-object confidence and a degradation state on the interface the Tier-1 specifies; The Tier-1 arbitrates the warning cascade and owns the braking decision and its safety case. Buyer: Tier-1 ADAS system engineer · functional-safety manager · OEM chief engineer Gate: A braking Tier-1 accepts the interface, diagnostics, safety assumptions and validation plan in writing, with a recorded go/no-go. Risk: No published ISO 26262 pathway. Until an assessor is engaged, the integrator is comparing a certified incumbent with an uncertified newcomer, and no perception result closes that gap.

chunks.title: UC-02 Nuisance-alert suppression
chunks.text: Nuisance-alert suppression. Standard: AIS-162 §6.8 false-reaction test. Dates: Gates every AEBS approval from 1 Jan 2027. Challenge: Four rivals already claim India tuning. India-native is no longer a differentiator. What no competitor has published is a measured nuisance rate — and AIS-162 tests for exactly that. What Deepgrid supplies: The denominator rather than the headline: a scenario-stratified false-positive rate per 1,000 km against a named baseline, on the same silicon class, the same functions and the same test set. Steps: Define the India nuisance set — overtaking two-wheelers, cut-in three-wheelers, cattle, roadside encroachment, unlit stationary trucks, wrong-way traffic, kerbside vending; Log every trigger and every non-trigger with scenario tags across three paid pilots, with telemetry rights secured in the contract; Score false positives per 1,000 km and true-positive recall, stratified by scenario, lighting and monsoon; Publish at equal scope; withhold any comparison that silently changes what is being compared. Buyer: Head of Validation · Tier-1 evaluation engineer · fleet safety manager Gate: One published equal-scope benchmark with scenario-stratified denominators and an independent agency’s protocol. Risk: A nuisance rate without a denominator is marketing. If scenario mix, kilometres and baseline are not fixed in advance, the result will be discounted to zero in a Tier-1 review.

chunks.title: UC-03 Blind-spot and moving-off information
chunks.text: Blind-spot and moving-off information. Standard: AIS-186 · AIS-187 · CMVR 125Q(2)–(3). Dates: 1 Oct 2027 new models · 1 Jan 2028 all models. Challenge: Two-wheeler riders were 46.2% of India’s 1,77,175 road deaths in 2024 and pedestrians 20.6%. AIS-186 demands an information signal 15 m before the expected collision point and forbids manual deactivation. What Deepgrid supplies: One India-trained perception core with two output contracts — near-field side and near-field front. Same silicon, same corpus, different detection geometry and signal timing. Steps: Side and front near-field cameras into the module; classify pedestrian, adult cyclist and child cyclist; Project turn geometry including the counter-turn; raise the signal at least 15 m before the collision point and hold it through the manoeuvre; Detect VRUs crossing at 3–5 km/h and cyclists parallel at 0–10 km/h inside the 3.7 m plane; hold through standstill until 15 m past the stopping point; Pass the false-information tests, including the traffic-sign case. Buyer: OEM cab and body engineer · Tier-1 HMI owner · fleet safety officer · driver Gate: A characterised near-field result against both test geometries, with the false-information cases run, from an independent agency rather than a bench demo. Risk: The signal cannot be switched off, so a high nuisance rate is permanently in the driver’s peripheral vision. UC-02 is a prerequisite, not a parallel track.

chunks.title: UC-04 Driver drowsiness and attention
chunks.text: Driver drowsiness and attention. Standard: AIS-184 (DDAWS) · CMVR 125Q(1). Dates: 1 Oct 2027 new models · 1 Jan 2028 all models. Challenge: Approval is not a track test. The manufacturer must run at least ten participants, none from the development team, in day and night, generating ten or more true-positive or false-negative events, and report per-participant sensitivity. What Deepgrid supplies: An in-cab drowsiness pipeline delivered together with the study that makes it approvable. The differentiator is not the model — it is handing the integrator a completed documentation package instead of a demonstration. Steps: In-cab infrared camera into the module: eyelid closure, gaze, head pose and PERCLOS-class metrics, working at night; Fuse with vehicle signals — reduced steering micro-corrections paired with larger, faster ones, and lateral lane-position variability; Warn above KSS level 8; escalate visual then acoustic per the HMI specification; Run the ten-participant study and deliver metrics, thresholds, activation speed, weather limits and the statistical analysis. Buyer: Fleet safety manager · driver · OEM homologation engineer · testing-agency assessor Gate: A completed ten-participant day-and-night study with per-participant sensitivity and standard deviation, plus the assessable documentation package. Risk: Intra-city, school and double-decker buses are outside scope unless the maker opts in. Sizing against all M2/M3 volume overstates this, and an urban-bus fleet is the wrong first pilot.

chunks.title: UC-05 Lane departure warning
chunks.text: Lane departure warning. Standard: AIS-188 (LDWS) · CMVR 98(6). Dates: 1 Oct 2027 new models · 1 Jan 2028 all models. Challenge: 58.6% of 2024 road deaths were on national and state highways — about 5% of the network — and 67.6% of accidents happened on straight roads, precisely where LDWS applies. Yet markings on those corridors are worn, inconsistent or absent. What Deepgrid supplies: Lane estimation that does not depend on a painted line: road edge, kerb, median, worn marking and vehicle-flow cues fused into a drivable-corridor estimate, with thresholds that move with traffic density and speed. Steps: Segment lane marking, road edge, kerb and median, and estimate marking quality; Estimate the drivable corridor and lateral position when no marking is visible; Modulate the departure threshold by traffic density and speed; suppress during indicated manoeuvres; Emit the departure event with confidence, plus an explicit temporarily-unavailable state. Buyer: OEM chassis and ADAS engineer · Tier-1 integrator · long-haul driver Gate: A measured corridor-estimation and alert result on unmarked and degraded Indian highway sections, reporting availability rate alongside false-alert rate. Risk: Declaring the function unavailable too readily is the easy way to pass a nuisance target and the fast way to fail type approval. Both numbers must be reported together or neither means anything.

chunks.title: UC-06 Government and PSU perception kit
chunks.text: Government and PSU perception kit. Standard: PPP-MII Order 2017 (rev. 2020) · GFR 153(iii). Dates: Transactable now — does not wait for 2027. Challenge: The shipping product is an FPGA module. Qualified volume silicon lands H1 2028 — after the mandate’s all-models date — and OEM design-in runs 18 to 30 months. Every rupee before H1 2028 has to come from the FPGA module. What Deepgrid supplies: The module packaged as a GeM-listed Class-I local-content perception kit for state transport undertakings and PSU fleets, where the gate is eligibility rather than certification. Steps: Compute and document local content at or above 50%, self-certified with the locations of value addition; List on GeM with country of origin and local-content percentage, qualifying for the Make in India filter; Bid into STU, PSU and municipal tenders reserved for or preference-weighted toward Class-I suppliers; Instrument every delivered unit and secure telemetry rights in the supply contract — these units are the evidence engine for UC-02. Buyer: STU procurement officer · depot engineer · Deepgrid BD · Head of Validation Gate: A live GeM listing with documented local content at or above 50%, and one Class-I tender bid submitted with telemetry rights in the draft contract. Risk: An incumbent already draws about 30% of revenue from government tenders and can underbid on empanelment. Class-I status is winnable but slowly, and a nodal ministry may prescribe local content above 50%.

chunks.title: What Deepgrid sells, and what it does not
chunks.text: Deepgrid sells a bounded camera-perception subsystem inside an accountable integrator’s safety case. It does not own brake actuation, calibration, homologation or warranty — and no use case may be written as if it does. Capital is not for: A full-stack braking safety case · broad OEM customisation · a radar programme of any kind · any performance marketing not backed by a measured result. Release capital only when partner access, field telemetry and a primary qualification artifact clear together.. Sequence: Now – 30 days: GeM listing prepared · nuisance taxonomy and protocol drafted with ARAI or ICAT · ISO 26262 assessor engaged as a procurement action (CEO · CTO); 30 – 60 days: Technical exchange opened with a braking Tier-1 · three paid pilots contracted with telemetry rights · drowsiness study cohort assembled (CEO · Validation); 60 – 90 days: First stratified nuisance result published · first Class-I bid submitted · written go/no-go recorded from the Tier-1 exchange (Validation · BD).

chunks.title: Slide 1 · Cover
chunks.text: Cover. Product Lines Fifteen SKUs, explained For each product: what it is, how it works on the shared silicon, who buys it, and what it contributes. 15 SKUs FOUR SLIDES EACH One chip SoC2 · 28 NM All figures are management projections prepared for fundraising purposes. August 2026 Fifteen products. One chip. This is the long version — every SKU in the plan, what it physically is, how it runs on shared silicon, who pays for it, and what it contributes. Everything here is a management projection prepared for fundraising.

chunks.title: Slide 2 · How to read this deck
chunks.text: How to read this deck. Every SKU gets the same four slides Learn the pattern once and you can navigate all fifteen products. DEEPGRID SEMI · PRODUCT LINES · MANAGEMENT PROJECTIONS 02 A · What it is If you held one, what would you be holding B · How it works What the silicon actually does in this product C · Who buys it Buyer, channel and the trigger to purchase D · How it fits What it contributes and what it depends on PART SKUS FY2032 REVENUE SHARE ROLE IN THE PORTFOLIO Road autonomy 3 ₹762 Cr 67.5% Three kits, one chip, ₹762 Cr Silicon & compute 5 ₹194 Cr 17.2% Selling the chip, not the vehicle Fleet & mobility 2 ₹88.7 Cr 7.9% Highest revenue per unit we sell Sensors & robotics 5 ₹83.5 Cr 7.4% Capability, channel and a second cycle The one thing to carry through Every SKU here runs the same SoC2 silicon under different firmware — one tapeout, not fifteen independent product bets. Each product gets the same four slides, in the same order: what it is, how it works, who buys it and why now, and how it fits. Four of them get two more, because a working simulator exists and you should watch it rather than take our word. Learn the pattern once and the next eighty slides navigate themselves.

chunks.title: Slide 3 · Why now
chunks.text: Why now. The mandate is a demand floor, not a forecast Compliance dates are set. The buying decision is when, not whether. DEEPGRID SEMI · PRODUCT LINES · MANAGEMENT PROJECTIONS 03 1.0 M TRUCKS A YEAR IN SCOPE 0.5 M NEW BUILD, ANNUALLY 0.5 M EXISTING FLEET RETROFIT 18,000 OUR FY2032 AD2 UNITS MAR 2025 Rule notified Sets the ADAS obligation for N2/N3 vehicles APR 2026 New models Drowsiness, blind-spot and lane-departure required OCT 2026 Existing models Obligation reaches the in-service fleet OCT 2027 Braking Advanced emergency braking on a separate schedule What a floor means for an investor A mandated purchase removes the hardest question in hardware — whether the buyer will pay for safety. Execution risk stays ours: certification and installation throughput. The demand is legislated, not forecast. Driver-drowsiness, blind-spot and lane-departure obligations land on new and existing commercial vehicles on fixed dates. About a million trucks a year fall in scope. For a fleet operator the question is not whether to buy — it is whose chip is inside when they do.

chunks.title: Slide 4 · The move
chunks.text: The move. One chip, priced for the mandate A phased 28 nm programme: prove the blocks, then the die, then commit the mask. DEEPGRID SEMI · PRODUCT LINES · MANAGEMENT PROJECTIONS 04 $3.17 M PROGRAMME COST $3.88 COST PER DIE 175k DIES TO REPAY IT 4 GATED STAGES Block prototypes Compute and radar blocks on a shared wafer Full-die prototype 57 mm² device, shared wafer Backend to GDSII Physical design and sign-off Production mask Committed only once silicon works Why this is the thing to fund Silicon absorbs 66.2% of the equity round, and every SKU in this deck is downstream of it. Sign-off and the mask are committed only after working silicon exists. The whole plan is downstream of one 28 nanometre part, and the programme is deliberately gated. Prove the compute and radar blocks first. Then the full die. Then backend sign-off. The production mask — the largest single commitment — is only paid for once working silicon exists.

chunks.title: Slide 5 · The silicon
chunks.text: The silicon. What the part actually is One 28 nm die under every SKU in this deck. Configuration changes; the compute does not. DEEPGRID SEMI · PRODUCT LINES · MANAGEMENT PROJECTIONS 05 PARAMETER SPECIFICATION WHY AN INVESTOR SHOULD CARE Process TSMC 28 nm · single die, ~57 mm² Monolithic, not chiplet — less cost and less risk. Compute 32,768 MACs at 600 MHz · 39.3 TOPS 64 compute cubes of 512 MACs. Derived, not rounded up. Memory 102.4 GB/s dual-channel LPDDR5 Bandwidth, not TOPS, binds multi-camera fusion. Transformer Hardware softmax · weight-stationary attention The operation an FPGA cannot do at frame rate. Safety Lockstep cores plus a hardware root of trust The path to an automotive safety rating. Throughput Eleven sensor channels fused in 8.6 ms Of a 33.3 ms frame budget — 74% left unused. The one number that explains the portfolio A part that clears eleven channels in a quarter of its frame budget configures downward into a one-channel module, a mirror unit, a radar pod or a forklift kit without redesigning the compute. That headroom is why fifteen SKUs are one tapeout, not fifteen programmes. Here is the part itself. Thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight multiply-accumulate units at six hundred megahertz, a hundred and two gigabytes a second of memory bandwidth, hardware softmax, and lockstep cores for the automotive safety path. chunks.text: The ask.  Fifteen products, one tapeout. The demand is legislated, the margin sits in silicon that needs no installation capacity, and no line in the plan requires us to win its market. chunks.title: One die, fifteen products
chunks.text: A six-chiplet 28 nm automotive SoC, taped out in gated stages, sold as fifteen products into a market where the demand date is written into law. ₹1,128 Cr of FY2032 revenue rests on one tapeout — which is the whole investment case, and the whole risk. The summary, if you read nothing else Deepgrid Semi is a one-chip company with fifteen ways to sell the same die. The chip is real — six RTL designs are tapeout-ready, a 130 nm tapeout is already done, and the perception stack runs at 40 fps on an FPGA today. The demand is real — India is writing ADAS into law for commercial vehicles, function by function, on dated deadlines. What is not yet reconciled is the schedule between them. Qualified silicon lands H1 2028 , after the last mandate date, and OEM design-in runs 18–30 months. So the next two years are an FPGA business sold through government and PSU channels — and that, not the ₹1,128 Cr terminal year, is what this round actually underwrites. Underwrite this — 01: Two products carry 64% of revenue. The truck kit and the smart mirror are one family sold to overlapping buyers. A certification delay hits ₹720 Cr at once. Underwrite this — 02: The FPGA window, not the ASIC. Nothing beyond FY2027’s ₹1.7 Cr happens without production silicon, and silicon arrives after every mandate date. Underwrite this — 03:

chunks.text: Three headline claims fail the company’s own controls. The mandate date, the ₹1 Cr defence revenue and the price comparison are all barred by its internal ledger — and printed anyway. The ask. Release capital against silicon, certification and paying customers. The $3.17M of tapeout NRE is already structured as four gates, and six of nine de-risking milestones are marked done before the round opens — so the forecast is the consequence of those gates, not the thing being funded. The argument in seven moves Demand is written into law Five ADAS functions become mandatory on commercial vehicles across 2027–28. Roughly a million N2/N3 units a year fall in scope. Foreign silicon prices India out An imported ADAS module costs multiples of the kit price this market can pay, and no indigenous alternative exists at this stage. So own the die Six chiplets on one 57 mm² part. Eleven sensor channels fused in 8.6 ms of a 33.3 ms frame. The headroom is the portfolio 74% of the frame is unused, so fifteen products across four surfaces run on one mask and one firmware stack. But the silicon arrives late Qualified parts land H1 2028 — after every mandate date on the calendar — and design-in runs 18–30 months. This is the turn in the argument. So the FPGA window is the strategy Government and PSU units ship first, and the telemetry they generate is what makes the Tier-1 design-in winnable.

chunks.title: An autonomous systems company that builds its own silicon
chunks.text: Deepgrid Semi sells complete, certified autonomy systems. It builds the six-chiplet die underneath them because owning the chip is the only way to ship those systems at a price the Indian market can pay. Founded and led by Aravind Prasad G (20 years, multiple exits — Evolgence IT Solutions, Deepgrid Datacentre, Evolgence Energy), with Ayaz Khan as silicon architecture lead. Incorporated in Telangana (CIN U62099TS2024PTC183631), operating from T-Hub Phase 2, Knowledge City, Hyderabad. Thirty-four people today, 541 in the FY2032 plan. Angels are domain operators, including DFT and semiconductor engineers backing the company personally. The order of markets is deliberate: commercial fleets are the mandate wedge and are live now; OEM design-in is the platform prize; defence and robotics is optionality on the same silicon that is already earning revenue. About 88% of planned revenue is systems and products ; roughly 5% is merchant silicon. Why now

source.heading: An autonomous systems company that builds its own silicon

chunks.title: The demand is legislated, not forecast
chunks.text: India is putting ADAS into law for commercial vehicles function by function, each with its own standard and its own date. Read at the standards level — the version that survives diligence — the schedule is this: AEBS (AIS-162, CMVR 96(12)) binds new models 1 Jan 2027 and all models 1 Oct 2027; drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off and lane-departure warning (AIS-184/186/187/188, CMVR 125Q and 98(6)) bind new models 1 Oct 2027 and all models 1 Jan 2028. The financial model sizes the reachable pool at ~500k new N2/N3 units a year plus a ~500k retrofit pool — 1.0M units . Four functions arriving on one clock is the commercial fact that matters. Every CV maker must source drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off and lane-departure together, so a supplier that carries more than one of the four from a single perception core is materially easier to nominate than four separate suppliers. That, rather than any single function, is the design-in argument. Three further rules stack on top of the truck mandate. AIS-140 requires GPS and driver-behaviour monitoring on commercial fleets — the S100 chiplet carries that telematics interface natively, in every kit, at no added cost. AIS-004 puts LDWS, FCWS and LKAS on all new M-category vehicles, creating aftermarket retrofit pull for the ₹50,000 mirror. And post-2022 supply fragility has Indian OEMs actively seeking a domestic chip partner.

chunks.title: Six chiplets, one 57 mm² die, six independent revenue lines
chunks.text: This is the asset the round buys. Each chiplet is a separate business, and replicating the set would take six tapeouts. 32,768 MACs at 600 MHz gives a derived 39.3 TOPS INT8 — architecture arithmetic, not a silicon measurement — with 102.4 GB/s of LPDDR5 bandwidth. The headroom is the product strategy: a drone stack, a wearable, a port AGV and a licensable core all fit inside the frame the truck kit leaves empty. PrimeSoC returned FEASIBLE on the architecture in March 2026. Two claims underneath that are worth separating from the TOPS number, because they are the ones competitors cannot patch around. Batch-dispatch firmware (Patent 1) decouples inference from RISC-V host supervision, keeping the ALU active far longer per cycle — the company’s answer to why headline TOPS on competing parts does not translate into delivered frames. And the R100’s 12-bit native radar ADC preserves dynamic range that every competitor re-quantises to INT16, which is what buys detection sensitivity in monsoon and fog. What it sees

chunks.title: The option the business buys you, deliberately not funded by this round
chunks.text: SoC4-A is the next-generation part: 1,024 tiles on a finer node, packaged four to a 4U liquid-cooled chassis for 16.76 PFLOPS FP4 peak and ~12 PFLOPS sustained at 1,120 W, with 256 GB of LPDDR5X. The pitch is sovereign AI inference — on-premise compute for Indian and GCC government, telecom and BFSI buyers whose data cannot leave the jurisdiction — plus robotaxi fleet compute and telecom edge. Two reasons it belongs in an investor summary and not in the plan. It is funded from operating profit , not from this round — the model already carries a SoC4 5 nm tapeout programme as an expense line growing to ₹169 Cr by FY2032. And it is the clearest statement of what the company thinks it is: not an ADAS supplier that happens to own a die, but a design team that can aim the same architecture at a different market without starting over. Price it as optionality. SoC2 is the business; this is the option the business buys you.

chunks.text: Six use cases carry the commercial plan. Five are regulated functions a truck maker must source; the sixth is the only arena that can transact before qualified silicon exists. The bounding statement Deepgrid sells a bounded camera-perception subsystem inside an accountable integrator’s safety case. It does not own brake actuation, calibration, homologation or warranty — and no use case may be written as if it does. That sentence is the most investor-relevant line in the whole file. It is what makes the Tier-1 sale possible, it caps the liability the company carries, and abandoning it is what would make the sale impossible. Five mandated functions, and when the silicon arrives Four of the five functions bind on one clock, which is the design-in argument: a CV maker must source them together, so a supplier carrying several from one perception core is easier to nominate than four suppliers. And the silicon arrives in the last column — after every mandate date on the chart. The six below carry the commercial plan. chunks.title: The company has a mandate it cannot yet serve and a chip that arrives after it
chunks.text: The strategic decision How does Deepgrid bridge the ~24 months between the mandate wave and its own qualified silicon — and which lane compounds into the ₹1,128 Cr plan rather than merely surviving the gap? Four constraints bound every answer. Cash is ₹2.5 lakh , so the first lane must produce revenue in months, not years. The 15 provisional patents carry a March 2027 conversion deadline that no use-of-funds line pays for. No ISO 26262 assessor is engaged , which gates the highest-value lane entirely. And the post-raise team is ten engineers with a CTO who is not yet full-time — enough to run two lanes properly, not five. The plan implies a path without ever arguing for it. That is the gap this section closes: five lanes were available, and the reason to pick one is not that it is the only one, but that it is the only one whose output is the next lane's input.

chunks.title: Government and PSU wedge — sell the FPGA module where the gate is eligibility
chunks.text: List the module on GeM as a Class-I local-content perception kit and bid into state transport undertaking, PSU and municipal tenders. At ≥50% local content the company earns a 20% margin of purchase preference and a right to match. This is the only arena where the gate is eligibility , which Deepgrid can satisfy today, rather than certification, which it cannot. Upside: Revenue in months on hardware that already exists — and every delivered unit is an instrumented vehicle. Trade-off: Warning-only retrofit, price-competitive, and an incumbent already draws ~30% of its revenue from these tenders. What must be true: Local content on the real bill of materials clears 50%, and telemetry rights survive a public-procurement contract.

Trade-off: Nobody licences an unproven core, and licensing the core undercuts the systems business that is 88% of revenue. What must be true: Silicon has a track record first — which is precisely why the model already places this line in FY2029.

chunks.title: Run A for B, not A then B
chunks.text: Lead with the government wedge and open the Tier-1 exchange in the same month. The temptation is to read Option A as a way to survive until the real business starts. That is the wrong reading, and it costs the company its only open differentiator. The dossier is explicit that India-native perception is no longer a differentiator — four rivals already claim it. The one contest whose result is not yet written is the measured nuisance rate , because no competitor has published one. Producing that number needs instrumented vehicles running Indian roads with scenario tags applied at capture and telemetry rights secured in the contract. Option A is the only lane that generates exactly that — and the number it generates is the single strongest thing Deepgrid can put in front of the Tier-1 in Option B. So the sequencing is not defensive. Government units are the sensor network that produces the evidence that wins the design-in. Sequence them A-then-B and the data arrives too late to matter; run A for B and the pre-silicon window becomes the thing that makes the post-silicon business winnable.

chunks.title: The round clears self-funding by ₹10.1 crore, and both missing lines land inside it
chunks.text: Pricing the recommended path against the model’s own cash schedule produces one number that decides the round, and it is not the terminal year. Closing cash balance ₹ Cr · base case, from the model’s own runway schedule Axis capped at ₹50 Cr; the last two columns are clipped. The model’s verdict on this schedule is “funded to self-sustaining”, and on its own terms that is correct. But the trough is ₹10.098 Cr on a ₹45 Cr round — a 22% margin of safety, with no contingency line anywhere in the use of funds. The undrawn ₹10 Cr CGTMSE facility is not in this schedule, and is almost exactly the size of the trough. The decision threshold The round works if the two unfunded lines come in under roughly ₹10 crore combined and the CGTMSE facility is genuinely available to draw. Above that, this is a short round wearing a full one. Both lines land in FY2027–28, the same window as the ₹18 Cr and ₹10 Cr tapeout draws — patent conversion because the March 2027 deadline is fixed, and the functional-safety assessor because the Tier-1 exchange opens in month one. Neither can be deferred past the trough. Do not accept a term sheet before both are quoted. chunks.title: The scenario set tests the wrong variable
chunks.text: The model runs Bull, Bear and Downside by scaling revenue — 1.2×, 0.75×, 0.3× — and adjusting opex as a percentage of it. Every one of those is a demand test. But demand is the most defensible thing in this plan: it is legislated, the pools are sourced, and no line assumes more than 2% capture. The variable that actually breaks this company is schedule. A tapeout slip pushes qualified silicon past H1 2028 into a window where the mandate has already closed, the FPGA lane is competing on price, and the fixed cost block — payroll, R&D, the remaining mask commitment — keeps running at full rate because none of it is a function of revenue. That case is not modelled anywhere. Ask for two more scenarios before the term sheet: a six-month silicon slip , and a fixed-cost floor in which opex holds at plan while revenue misses. Those are the two that decide whether ₹45 Cr is the right number. Recommendation

chunks.title: Proceed — and re-cut the use of funds before the term sheet, not after
chunks.text: The case holds. The asset is real, the demand is legislated, the unit economics are the strongest part of the plan, and the staged tapeout already gives an investor four places to stop. Nothing found here argues against funding it. What it argues against is funding it on the current allocation . Four lines and no reserve, with a ₹10.1 Cr trough and two dated obligations that appear nowhere, is a use of funds that has not been asked the questions above. All four fixes are arithmetic, none of them changes the business, and all four are cheaper to make now than to discover in FY2029. 01 Quote and insert the two missing lines. Patent conversion by March 2027 and a functional-safety assessor. If they clear ₹10 Cr combined, the round is short and should be sized up rather than squeezed. Before term sheet 02 Reclassify the CGTMSE facility as declared contingency. It is not in the cash schedule and it is almost exactly the size of the trough. Calling it working capital hides the only reserve the plan has. Before term sheet 03 Re-forecast FY2027 without the ₹1.2 Cr defence assumption. Rebuild the first year from the delivered ₹23.01L plus the government lane, and show what the FPGA window actually earns. Before term sheet

chunks.title: Released against silicon, not against the forecast
chunks.text: ₹55 Cr of blended capital: ₹45 Cr of equity ($4.79M) for 18.07% at a ₹204 Cr pre-money, plus a ₹10 Cr collateral-free CGTMSE facility for working capital. Dilution is tied only to the milestone that creates enterprise value. Of the equity, 66% goes to tapeout NRE and IP , 16% to a 10-FTE engineering team over 18 months, 8% to AIS-162/188 type approval through ARAI/ICAT. The $3.17M of NRE is not one commitment. It is four, and each is a point where the next cheque can be withheld: Prove the blocks on a shared MPW Compute and radar DSP blocks, 5 mm² each, 100 samples $138K Full-die MPW prototype The complete 57 mm² part plus five prototype wafers $232K Backend to GDSII Physical design, DFT, integration and sign-off — only after the blocks work $1.00M Dedicated production mask The largest single commitment, paid only once silicon exists $1.00M Controller and PHY IP take the remaining $0.8M. At volume the die costs $3.88 — $2.38 of wafer against 1,010 good die per 300 mm wafer, plus $1.50 of assembly and test. NRE breaks even at 174,908 chips against a plan that ships ~217,000 dies through FY2032, and the mask is cut for a ~500,000-die lifetime, which is the volume commitment that earns the $2,400 wafer price the whole cost stack depends on.

chunks.title: Ten things to test, and where the documents disagree with each other
chunks.text: The materials argue their own risks rather than burying them, which is worth crediting. Three of the ten come from the company’s own claim-control ledger, and two are dated cash calls that appear in no allocation line — it already knows which headline numbers will not survive diligence, which is a good sign about the team and a bad sign about the memorandum. Ordered by what an investor acts on first. Structural Concentration — two products carry 64% of revenue: The truck kit (₹450 Cr, 40%) and the smart mirror (₹270 Cr, 24%) are the same family sold to overlapping buyers. A certification delay or a fitment bottleneck hits ₹720 Cr at once — more than the other thirteen lines combined. Structural The FPGA window, not the ASIC, is what the next two years are made of: Qualified volume silicon lands H1 2028 — after the all-models date — and OEM design-in runs 18 to 30 months. So line-fit revenue cannot come first, and every rupee before H1 2028 has to come from the FPGA module through government and PSU channels (UC-06). The plan’s own FY2027 line agrees: ₹1.7 Cr, FPGA only. An investor should underwrite the FPGA window explicitly rather than treating it as a run-up to the real business. Unfunded Fifteen provisional patents expire in March 2027 and nothing pays to convert them:

chunks.title: Ten things to test, and where the documents disagree with each other
chunks.text: The provisionals were filed March 2026 (IN2026/DGR/001–015) and must become complete specifications within twelve months of the priority date. The memorandum lists that expiry among its own four reasons to move — and then allocates nothing to it. This is a hard, dated cash call on the IP the entire thesis rests on , landing inside the round’s first year, and it appears in no line of the use of funds. Unfunded The ISO 26262 assessor gates the highest-value lane and is not in the budget: No functional-safety pathway is published, and until an assessor is engaged a Tier-1 is comparing a certified incumbent with an uncertified newcomer — a gap no perception result closes. The company’s own 30-day plan lists engaging one as a procurement action, but the use of funds carries AIS-162/188 type approval only . Ask for the quote and the line item before the term sheet, not after. Claim control Three regulatory timelines are in circulation, and only one survives: The memorandum and the financial model both anchor demand to GSR 184(E) from April 2026 . The company’s own claim controls list “an April 2026 mandate” and “GSR 184(E) as final law” as banned claims , and the standards-level dates are 2027–2028. This is not pedantry: it moves first mandated revenue by roughly eighteen months, and it is the first thing a diligence team with a regulatory adviser will check.

chunks.title: Ten things to test, and where the documents disagree with each other
chunks.text: Claim control The ₹1 Cr defence-revenue claim does not survive its own claim controls: It appears on the memorandum cover and in the model’s historical context. The internal ledger substantiates ₹23.01L delivered and ₹78.39L at L1 stage — lowest bidder, not an award — sitting in a different legal entity (Deepgrid Datacentre Pvt Ltd) with the IP owned by MCEME. The delivered revenue is real and is genuine proof the stack works before silicon; the headline is not the number to put in front of an investor. Document The two totals in circulation are ₹1,128 Cr and ₹1,388 Cr: They differ by ₹259.5 Cr across eleven product lines that the business plan carries and the financial model does not size. This is not only a document-to-document gap: the information memorandum’s own revenue slide is headed ₹1,128 Cr while its tables sum to ₹1,388 Cr. Pick one before the data room opens; the model is the conservative document and the one this summary follows. Document Tapeout NRE is quoted at both $2.42M and $3.17M: The die card says $2.42M; the platform slide says “a single $3.17M tapeout”; the model’s use-of-funds says $3.17M phased across four gates. A $750K difference in the single largest line item is the first thing a diligence team will price. Same for the addressable pool — 5M+ trucks in the memorandum against 1.0M in the model.

chunks.title: Ten things to test, and where the documents disagree with each other
chunks.text: Claim control The compute-box line should not be underwritten on price: Published module pricing for embedded edge-AI parts does not support a price-advantage claim for the A100 SKUs, several of which carry fewer channels than comparably priced alternatives. The defensible positions are domestic supply, India-tuned perception and deployed-system cost — and a like-for-like deployed comparison is a diligence deliverable, not a slide. The company’s own claim controls bar quoting any competitor per-unit price, which the memorandum’s pricing slide does anyway. Structural Key-person exposure on both sides of the company: The founder is the single point of commercial accountability across all four business units and holds 95.6% of shares. The CTO — architect of the matrix ALU and author of the radar RTL — is not yet full-time , with the plan showing Q1 FY28. Separately, the cap table totals 102,797 shares against the 100,890 used in the pricing basis, a 1,907-share difference to reconcile before term sheet.

chunks.title: Ten things to test, and where the documents disagree with each other
chunks.text: Two things that were flagged earlier and now resolve cleanly. The “six cameras” versus “eleven channels” question is a difference of scope, not an error: the AD2 kit is specified at six cameras, and the compute box ingests eleven channels (7 RGB + 2 thermal + 2 radar) in the same 8.6 ms. And prior capital is deployed, not banked : ₹48 lakh of grants (ARAI ₹36L, HDFC Parivartan ₹12L) and ~₹2 Cr of angel funding are fully spent, which is why the ₹2.5 lakh cash position is a date, not a number. Release capital against silicon, certification and paying customers — the four tapeout gates are already structured as tranches, and six of the nine de-risking milestones are marked done before the round opens. The forecast is the consequence of those gates, not the thing being funded. chunks.title: The bounding statement
chunks.text: DeepGrid sells a bounded camera-perception subsystem inside an accountable integrator's safety case. It does not own brake actuation, calibration, homologation or warranty, and no use case below may be written as if it does. Do not fund: A full-stack braking safety case · broad OEM customisation · a radar programme of any kind · any performance marketing not backed by a measured result. Release capital only when partner access, field telemetry and a primary qualification artifact clear together.

chunks.text: Press Release January 06, 2026 Scalable, turn-key solution tailored for India’s traffic and road conditions, delivers safe navigation and cost-effective regulatory compliance. Integrates Aptiv’s latest radar and smart camera—featuring STRADVISION’s AI-based vision technology—with Aptiv’s modular software solutions, all optimized for commercial vehicle applications. SCHAFFHAUSEN, Switzerland — Aptiv PLC (NYSE: APTV), a global industrial technology company, today announced that a leading commercial vehicle OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) has selected its Gen 6 Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS) to equip its future trucks and buses in India. This agreement marks Aptiv’s first collaboration with an Indian commercial vehicle OEM on ADAS. It comes as the industry prepares for 2027 regulations requiring new trucks and buses to include safety features such as automatic emergency braking, lane departure and blind spot warnings and pedestrian and obstacle detection when starting from a stop. To meet these requirements, commercial vehicle OEMs face unique challenges. They must integrate advanced safety technologies across diverse vehicle types and powertrains, address larger blind spots, and ensure reliability in harsh environments. chunks.title: Verdict
chunks.text: The arithmetic is clean. Every stated capture % reproduces exactly from its own formula, and the revenue build ties to the P&L to the rupee (₹1,128.45 Cr FY32, 15 lines). The problem is not the numbers — it is that one column silently mixes two incompatible denominators, and the product the whole story rests on is the one using the flattering basis. The tab's own closing claim — "our FY32 volumes are a single-digit share of each pool" — is false for AD2 on the sheet's own dominant methodology and its own stated TAM.

chunks.title: Finding 2 — On its own revenue basis, AD2 is 23.9%, not 1.8%
chunks.text: AD2 is the mandate story: 18,000 units, ₹450 Cr, 40% of FY32 revenue. - As shown: 18,000 ÷ 1,000,000 units = 1.8% - On the sheet's dominant basis: ₹450 Cr = $47.9M against the sheet's own row 8, "TAM — mandated ADAS (AIS-184/186/187/188) annual = $200M" → 23.9% Both use the sheet's own numbers. A 13x swing rests on a choice the sheet never states. 23.9% of a regulated market by FY32 is a defensible plan — but it is a different plan from the one "1.8%" describes, and it invites a different diligence question.

chunks.title: Finding 3 — The 1.0M SAM adds a flow to a stock
chunks.text: Row 9 builds SAM as ~500k new/yr + ~500k retrofit. The first is an annual flow; the second is a one-time stock of existing N2/N3 vehicles, mandated from Oct 2026. By FY32 — five years into the retrofit window — that stock is substantially converted, so it should not still sit in an FY32 denominator at full value. On the annual flow alone, AD2 capture is 3.6%.

chunks.title: Finding 4 — Two sheets disagree on whether AD0 is mandate-driven
chunks.text: AD0 is 54,000 units and ₹270 Cr — 24% of FY32 revenue, the second-largest line. - Revenue Build J44 labels it: "AD0 Smart Mirror (mandate retrofit)" - Demand & TAM row 17 says: "NOT mandated — voluntary safety/convenience buy" Mandate-driven and voluntary demand carry different risk, different sales cycles, and different defensibility. chunks.title: What to change before this goes in front of an investor
chunks.text: 1. Split the column in two — Capture % (revenue) and Capture % (units) — or convert everything to revenue ÷ revenue. Do not leave one header over two metrics. 2. Show AD2 on the revenue basis and defend 23.9%. The mandate is the strongest thing in this plan. A sophisticated reader will recompute it, find 23.9%, and wonder why 1.8% was the number on the page. Leading with 23.9% and the mandate floor is the stronger position. 3. Split SAM into flow and stock with a retrofit-conversion curve, so the FY32 denominator is an FY32 denominator. 4. Resolve the AD0 mandate question and make both sheets say the same thing. 5. Size the remaining four, or say plainly they are unsized — and add T100.

chunks.title: BLUF
chunks.text: Four findings change the deck. Two correct errors I introduced, one strengthens the case, one weakens a stated strength. 1. The deck flags a mandate-date conflict that does not exist. Slide 27 says the verification "carries two different 2027 dates — pin the exact instrument and date." The gazette resolves it: 1 January 2027 (new models) and 1 October 2027 (all models) are one two-stage timetable under rule 96(12), not a contradiction. Ask #8 and next-step #10 should be deleted, and the instrument named: G.S.R. 834(E), 11 Nov 2025, amending G.S.R. 184(E) which was only ever a draft. 2. The "~20× the compliance anchor" comparison is cross-scope and overstates the gap against DeepGrid's own interest. It sets a ₹2.50L capital purchase against a device sticker price. Against the AIS-140 three-year total cost of ownership — ₹22,400 basic / ₹40,600 standard / ₹62,200 enterprise — the like-for-like ratio is 4.0×–11.2×, not ~20×. The pricing contest is materially less lopsided than the deck says, and the correction favours the company. 3. "2.8–6.5× cheaper than imports" cannot be verified and should be demoted. No public per-unit India price exists for Mobileye EyeQ6, Bosch/Continental, Qualcomm SA8295 or Nvidia Orin. bitsensing — the one comparable product with a live India launch —

chunks.title: The one thing that survives untouched, and it matters
chunks.text: No vendor in the cohort holds Indian ADAS certification — and AIS-162 itself is still listed as "Draft" on the MoRTH AIS register. The deck's central competitive claim — "the window is the asset here, not the price gap" — is the claim that survived this run best. It is also the claim that does not depend on any price. That is the argument to lead with. The price gap is unverifiable; the certification window is real and documented.

chunks.title: What the pricing evidence actually implies for the commercial thesis
chunks.text: The AIS-140 precedent is the closest domestic analogue and it points somewhere specific: over three years, the platform licence can exceed hardware cost by 2–3×. Value in that market went to whoever held the recurring compliance relationship, not to whoever sold the box. Combined with the ~8-year notification-to-enforcement lag on AIS-140, this supports two things the deck already argues and one it does not: - supports the transitional-enforcement reading (slide 6) - supports "price the function, not the bundle" (slide 30) - not yet in the deck: it argues for AD3 (the rented kit) being the strategically right commercial model rather than the pricing anomaly slide 31 currently calls it. The ₹0.66 Cr/yr figure still does not reconcile at ~26× the outright sale — but the direction (recurring over capital) is what the domestic precedent rewards.

chunks.title: Contested, not resolved: the FY32 margin basis
chunks.text: A prior run derived 77.2% as the honest blended FY32 gross margin at a 72% kit margin. Reproducing it here: 77.2% blended requires 87.2% gross margin on the ₹474.30 Cr of non-ADAS revenue. That is not more defensible than the deck's flat 72% — it simply moves the assumption from "non-ADAS earns what the kit earns" to "non-ADAS earns 87.2%", and neither is disclosed anywhere in BP-1A. Recommendation: show the range, not a point. FY32 EBITDA is ₹309 Cr to ₹381 Cr depending on non-ADAS margin (72% → 87.2%), with attributable earnings of ₹19.6 Cr to ₹24.2 Cr. Both ends still sit far below the stated ₹536.63 Cr, so the 120% impossibility finding on slide 15 is unaffected — only the rebuilt figure widens.

chunks.title: Source bias — stated plainly
chunks.text: The AIS-140 price evidence (EV-09 … EV-13) comes predominantly from fleetx, a fleet telematics vendor publishing buyer guides. Three of four price rows trace to one commercial publisher with an interest in emphasising total cost of ownership over sticker price. That bias runs in the same direction as the finding it supports — a telematics vendor benefits from readers concluding the box is more expensive than it looks. The finding is therefore directionally suspect and is labelled medium confidence, not high, and the deck should attribute it rather than assert it. Corroboration from a non-telematics source (an RTO circular, an operator association, a fleet's own procurement note) is the single highest-value next retrieval.

chunks.title: Decision: no composite competitor score is issued
chunks.text: The contract fails a run where "scores or charts use undefined metrics" and where "source coverage is uneven but confidence is hidden". Both conditions would apply to a ranked competitor score here: - 4 of 7 cohort members have unit price = UNVERIFIED (EV-20 … EV-23) - 0 of 7 hold Indian ADAS certification (EV-08 and the deck's own table) - the two strongest India-present competitors found (bitsensing, ZF WABCO) publish no unit price at all (EV-16) A weighted score across those inputs would rank source availability, not competitive position, and would then be charted as if it were the latter. chunks.title: A1 — The regulation is cited wrongly, and the deck contradicts itself · CRITICAL
chunks.text: Slide 4 says naming GSR 184e in client-facing material is "defensible" and that the "gazette notification itself" is outstanding. Slide 12 says "Stop any external claim citing G.S.R.184(E) as final law." Both are in the same delivered deck. Slide 12 is right. G.S.R. 184(E) (20 Mar 2025) was only ever a draft. The notified instrument is G.S.R. 834(E), 11 Nov 2025, amended by G.S.R. 862(E), gazetted 21 Nov 2025 — and its own preamble names 184(E) as the draft it supersedes ( EV-REG-02 ). The gazette is not outstanding; it has been public for nine months. The strings "834" and "862" appear nowhere in the 83 slides. Root cause: Round 2's live research took ZF's press note and Aptiv's release — both of which repeat "GSR 184e" ( EV-ZF-05 ) — as corroboration of the instrument. Vendors repeating a draft is not evidence of law. A prior run had already read the gazette text; that finding was overwritten by a weaker source. Fix: rewrite slide 4's regulatory row; add the instrument, both rule references and the two-stage timetable; keep slide 12's stop-rule and make it consistent.

chunks.title: A2 — Starkenn's headline number cannot be stated · HIGH
chunks.text: "2,500+ vehicles" appears on slides 19, 20 and 83 — including the hostile-question slide ("Starkenn shows 2,500+ vehicles. Are we not already behind?"). The single source behind it (YourStory, Nov 2024) contains three mutually inconsistent figures in one interview: "over 2,500 vehicles", "over 700 units sold", and "300+ vehicles have deployed our tech" ( EV-STK-04 ). The dossier propagated the largest. It is self-reported, un-audited and ~21 months old. Compounding it: Starkenn is a 57-person company, shrinking 15.8% YoY, with $2.0m of lifetime funding ( EV-STK-05 ) — none of which is in the deck. Fix: remove the number. Argue Starkenn from its 30% government-tender share and subscription model, which is the durable point, and answer the hostile question with the source contradiction rather than conceding it.

chunks.title: B3 — No distinction between systems that brake and systems that warn · CRITICAL
chunks.text: The dossier runs one heatmap across all competitors. But the market divides at brake actuation: - Reach actuation (AEBS): ZF, Aptiv+STRADVISION — can satisfy rule 96(12) - Warning-only: drivebuddyAI (camera-only, alerts driver), bitsensing (explicitly no AEB), Starkenn — cannot satisfy rule 96(12) at any price These are two different markets, two different buyers and two different clocks. The warning-only group is winning retrofit fleet-safety budget today; the actuating group is competing for homologation budget in 2027. Flattening them makes drivebuddyAI look like a mandate competitor when it is not, and makes the mandate look nearer than it is.

Business line, product category, and revenue type each independently sum to the same total: 75.0 + 33.5 + 1229.5 + 50.0, and 75.0 + 33.5 + 153.0 + 966.2 + 110.3 + 50.0, and 75.0 + 1197.0 + 66.0 + 50.0. Stated on p.8 and reproduced on p.15. - The MicroDC-A1 spec block is internally coherent: 4 chips x 4.19 PF = 16.76 PFLOPS; 4 x 280 W = 1,120 W; 1,024 tiles x 4 = 4,096. - FY2027 revenue of 6.0 Cr reconciles between the P&L and the business-line table. - Traction claims are specific and dated: 15 provisional patents filed Mar 2026 (IN2026/DGR/001-015), 1 Cr defence revenue received Q1 2026 on FPGA hardware, YOLOv11n at 40fps measured on Artix-7 200T.

chunks.title: 2. What is being assumed
chunks.text: Assumptions presented in the document's own voice, with what would confirm each. - The mandate converts to purchases. GSR 184(E) is described as "a regulatory floor, not a forecast". Enforcement existing is not the same as fleets buying on schedule. Confirmed by: signed fleet orders, not the gazette notification. - ASIC economics arrive as modelled. Gross margin goes 53% - 88% between FY2027 and FY2032, resting on the FPGA-to-ASIC transition. Confirmed by: first silicon returning to spec, which the timeline places at Q4 2026. - Sales and marketing at 12–14% of revenue holds while revenue compounds from 6.0 Cr to 1,388.0 Cr — a 231x increase over five years on a roughly flat S&M ratio. Confirmed by: cost-per-design-win from the first fleet cohort. - "No indigenous alternative exists". Confirmed by: an independent scan, not by the company's own competitive slide. - The India-data moat compounds. Stated as structural. Confirmed by: a measured accuracy delta on Indian road data versus a foreign stack — a number the IM does not have.

chunks.title: 3.1 The headline revenue number is wrong, and it is on the cover — CRITICAL
chunks.text: Location Figure p.3 cover stat " ₹1,128 Cr — Revenue FY2032E" p.21 slide title "Revenue to ₹1,128 Crore by FY2032" p.5 platform cascade " ₹1,388 Cr by FY32" p.6 investment thesis "Total group revenue: ₹1,388 Cr FY32" p.20 P&L, FY2032 row " 1388.0 " p.21's own table, directly beneath its title sums to 1,388.0 A ₹260 Cr gap, 23% of the number. It appears on the cover — the most-read figure in the document — and again as a slide title contradicting the table printed under it. The ₹1,388 Cr figure is the supported one: three independent cross-tabs and the P&L agree.

chunks.title: 3.3 SAM exceeds TAM — structurally impossible
chunks.text: p.7: " ₹61,000 Cr India ADAS aftermarket TAM by 2030". p.14: "India SAM (5M+ trucks mandated) ₹85,000 Cr ". A serviceable available market cannot exceed the total addressable market it sits inside. p.14 also lists a "Retrofit market (9Cr vehicles) ₹4,50,000 Cr", which makes the ₹61,000 Cr TAM smaller than two other markets on the same page. Either the TAM is scoped far more narrowly than its label says, or the figures come from different definitions that were never reconciled.

chunks.title: 3.4 Die cost stated three different ways — on a slide about not confusing costs
chunks.text: Location Die cost p.4 "the die is ~$30, not $6,000" p.8 " <$3 die · ~$30 board BOM" p.22 headline " <$4 Die Cost (at 1M chips)" p.22 body, same box "Die ( $3 ) + carrier board + connectors + packaging = ~$30" p.4 has mistaken the board BOM for the die. p.22 is titled "Cost Clarity — Three Numbers VCs Always Confuse" and contradicts itself between its own headline and body. chunks.title: 3.5 NRE / tapeout cost: five figures, never reconciled

chunks.title: 3.6 Die area: 57.1mm² vs 42mm²
chunks.text: p.8, p.15 and p.6 all state ~ 57.1mm². p.16 states "68.7 effective TOPS on a 42mm² die". These are reconcilable — the six chiplet areas on p.15 (7+6+7+8+7+7) sum to exactly 42mm², so 42 is silicon area and 57.1 is the combo die. The document never says so, and p.16 calls 42mm² "a die". p.16 also introduces "68.7 effective TOPS" against 39.3 TOPS peak everywhere else, with no definition of "effective".

One Chip." · p.9: " 9 CAM + 2 RADAR FUSED", itemising 7x RGB + 2 thermal + 2 radar = 11 channels, no LiDAR, no ultrasonic · p.13 pricing: AD2 = " 6 Cam + 2 Radar + LiDAR + 4 US " · p.15: A100 is " 6-camera MIPI CSI-2". chunks.title: 3.10 The "3 to 7x cheaper" claim does not match its own table
chunks.text: p.14 claims " 3 to 7x Cheaper Than Every Import" and lists imports at ₹5–8L (Mobileye), ₹8–12L (Continental), ₹12–18L (Nvidia), ₹10–15L (Qualcomm) against DGrid at ₹2–2.5L. Worst case against the cheapest import: ₹5L / ₹2.5L = 2.0x, below the claimed floor of 3x. Best case against the dearest: ₹18L / ₹2L = 9.0x, above the claimed ceiling of 7x. chunks.title: 3.11 The 200x utilisation claim strains its own arithmetic
chunks.text: p.16 states competitors achieve " 1–5% hardware utilisation" and that DGrid's ALU is "active 200x longer per cycle". 200x of 1% is 200%, and of 5% is 1,000% — both impossible. The claim only works if the competitor baseline is at or below 0.5%, which is outside the range the same paragraph states.

chunks.title: C1. The mandate the whole thesis rests on is a draft that never became law
chunks.text: The IM's first reason to invest: "MoRTH GSR 184(E) enforcement is live — April 2026. Every N2/N3 truck sold after this date requires ADAS compliance… Regulatory floor, not a forecast." It repeats April 2026 on p.3, p.6, p.7 and p.26. G.S.R. 184(E) (20 Mar 2025) was only ever a draft notification. The notified rule is G.S.R. 834(E), 11 Nov 2025, in force 12 Nov 2025, amended by G.S.R. 862(E) of 21 Nov 2025. The binding dates are: System Standard New models All models AEBS + stability AIS-162 / IS 11852:2019 1 Jan 2027 1 Oct 2027 LDWS AIS-188 1 Oct 2027 1 Jan 2028 DDAWS / BSIS / MOIS AIS-184/186/187 (rule 125Q) 1 Oct 2027 1 Jan 2028 Independently corroborated outside this repo: Fortune India reports AEBS and stability control mandatory from 1 October 2027, and BSIS/MOIS/DDAWS/LDWS from 1 January 2028, notified vide GSR 834(E) dated 11 November 2025. MoRTH's own AIS register still lists AIS-162 with status "Draft". So there is no April 2026 mandate. There is no "regulatory floor" already live. The document's opening argument, its "Why Act Now" close, and its ₹61,000 Cr demand framing all rest on a superseded draft. This was already flagged. Prior work in this repo lists as an explicit st

chunks.title: C2. The ₹1 Cr defence revenue is misdescribed four ways
chunks.text: The IM states "₹1Cr Defence Revenue" on the cover, "₹1 Cr institutional defence revenue RECEIVED Q1 2026" on p.15, "₹1Cr Defence Revenue Received" as a completed milestone on p.18, and "₹1 Cr defence revenue already received" in the exit vectors on p.26. Prior verified work finds: ₹23.01L delivered (GeM Robot Training); ₹78.39L is L1 — lowest bidder, not an award; it sits in Deepgrid Datacentre Pvt Ltd, not Deepgrid Semi; and IP on the delivered contract is MCEME-owned under Clause 27. The company's own BP-1A states "none of it is trucking/ADAS revenue." Four separate problems in one number: 78% of it is not revenue, it is in a different legal entity than the one raising, the IP does not belong to the company, and none of it is ADAS. A single diligence question retires it.

chunks.title: C3. The competitor set omits every threat that prior work ranked highest
chunks.text: The IM names Mobileye, Bosch, Steradian, Horizon Robotics, Nvidia, Netrasemi, NXP, Mindgrove, Aurora, Kodiak, ABB/Kalmar, ideaForge, Apptronik and Agility, and asserts on p.19 that Indian competition is a "genuine open lane… the one unit where 'no Indian competitor' is unambiguously true." Not named, and ranked as the real threats: - ZF WABCO — ADAS already shipping as OE fitment with a leading Indian CV OEM, with an in-house Indian test track and homologation capability DeepGrid concedes it lacks. Prior work calls this the actual threat, "not Nvidia/Mobileye." - Starkenn — company-reported 2,500+ vehicles and 30% of revenue from government tenders, plus BrakeSafe radar AEBS; highest threat in the government/mining segment the IM treats as open. - drivebuddyAI — $2.5M contracted across 3,000 heavy trucks (May 2026), scope to 10,000. No longer demo-only. - bitsensing — India retrofit ADAS kit launched Feb 2026 with an IKIO channel MoU. - Gahan AI, Aptiv, STRADVISION, Sterling Tools × MINIEYE. Netrasemi's ₹107 Cr Series A also demotes "India-native" as a differentiator — domestic origin alone no longer distinguishes DeepGrid.

Six of 27 rows in a prior evidence ledger are UNVERIFIED and all six are import prices; bitsensing's "pricing agreed case by case" corroborates that this is market structure, not a search failure — automotive ADAS unit pricing is quoted, not listed. chunks.title: C5. The 88% gross margin is arithmetically unreachable
chunks.text: The IM projects 88% blended GM at FY2032. Prior analysis: 88.4% blended requires ~120% margin on all non-kit revenue. At 72% kit margin the honest blend is 77.2%. An 11-point GM error at FY2032 revenue of ₹1,388 Cr is roughly ₹150 Cr of gross profit, which flows straight to the ₹536.6 Cr EBITDA line the deck leads with.

chunks.title: Financial strengths (must survive the rebuild)
chunks.text: - Revenue built from unit volume × price per named product — makes the top line testable against capacity, channel and market size. - Selling prices held flat for six years; all growth comes from volume. - FY2027 presented honestly as an investment year at −30% EBITDA margin. - EBITDA and net income both turn positive in FY2028 — a short path to self-funding reduces capital at risk. - Segment definitions stated explicitly, so the revenue split is auditable. - Overheads scale smoothly rather than stepping.

chunks.title: Not findings
chunks.text: - 197% revenue CAGR. Ambition is the asset at this stage, and the plan decomposes growth into units and prices — the correct test, which it passes. - Flat six-year pricing. Reads as conservative. It matters only in combination with F-03/F-05, because it forces the whole margin burden onto cost. - Rounding drift ≤ ₹0.01 Cr across several P&L identities — inside the plan's own precision.

chunks.title: 1. BLUF
chunks.text: The segmentation in v3 is presentationally strong but not yet evidentially bottom-up, and three fixable defects — one arithmetic, one disclosure, one margin-mechanism — will surface in the first serious diligence pass. Fix them before the model circulates further; none require changing the plan's ambition.

chunks.title: 3. Tension
chunks.text: The model's own Reconciliation tab already documents that the June 2026 Information Memorandum, now in investors' hands, disagrees with it. Every week the current model circulates unreconciled, the number of counterparties holding two contradictory documents grows. Separately, the plan's nearest-term promise — EBITDA breakeven in FY2028 — rests on a 20-point gross-margin jump in a single year, and has only a 6.3-point cushion. That is the first thing an analyst stress-tests, and it is the claim closest to the money.

chunks.title: 4. Argument arc
chunks.text: 1. Context — v3 exists to segment a plan the company already believes in; company-level figures are unchanged by design. 2. Credit — the build is genuinely decomposed to units × ASP per product, which is better than most material at this stage. 3. Tension — but three defects are visible to any analyst in under an hour. 4. Proof A (arithmetic) — FY2028 net income contradicts the model's own EBT and tax lines, and understates the company's story. 5. Proof B (disclosure) — the IM and the model disagree in opposite directions on linked figures, so at least one was never re-derived. 6. Proof C (mechanism) — segment margins are identical to one decimal across three unrelated businesses; the mix defense is arithmetically unavailable (6% of the expansion), and the residual converts to a ₹27,500 kit BOM. 7. Implication — the fragile claim is near-term, not terminal: FY2028 breakeven, not FY2032 scale. 8. Action — a ranked fix list, sequenced by what each defect costs in diligence.

chunks.title: 6. Evidence map
chunks.text: Direct evidence (Verified — re-derived from the file): FY2028 net income break (₹2.29 Cr); segment totals vs P&L drift in FY30/FY31; identical per-segment margins; margin bridge 6%/94%; breakeven-GM cushions; FY2032 concentration; R&D-to-payroll ratio; absence of formulas, cash flow, uses of funds. Fair synthesis: the IM/model contradiction is documented in the workbook's own Reconciliation tab; characterizing it as disclosure exposure is synthesis. The ₹27,500 BOM is arithmetic; calling it implausible for compute + software + sensors is synthesis. Interpretation (Judgement — no external benchmark run): that 89% is unreachable for a bundled hardware kit; implied headcount at ₹25L loaded cost; that flat six-year ASPs understate price erosion. All are analyst opinion and must be labelled as such on the slide, not presented as benchmarked.
