chunks.title: 4. Retired claims still live in the prior deck
chunks.text: The prior deck is not clean. It asserts, on slide 31: "12.9× COST ADVANTAGE vs. Mobileye $50 ASP (sourced)" This is on the retired list — it compares their ASP to our die cost. It must not be carried forward into any new deck. It also states "₹1 Cr already received" with its own red-team flag that the nature of the revenue is unconfirmed. Later work resolved this: ₹23.01 lakh delivered, ₹78.39 lakh is L1 (lowest bidder, not an award), sitting in Deepgrid Datacentre — a different legal entity — with customer-owned IP, and none of it trucking or ADAS revenue. The prior deck's figure is ~4× the real one. My playbook's slide 14 ("What we are not claiming") is the only artifact in the set that gets this right. It should be carried into any merged deck unchanged.

chunks.title: Sterling Tools partners MINIEYE to accelerate ADAS and Driver Monitoring Solutions for India
chunks.text: By Aman Shukla 4 min read·Published on Jan 19, 2026 · 6:25 AM IST·Updated Jul 14, 2026 · 12:37 PM IST Share on FacebookShare on XShare on LinkedInShare on WhatsAppShare by email Listen to this article Speed1.0x -Advertisement- Sterling Tools Limited (BSE: 530759 \ NSE: STERTOOLS), a leading automotive components and technology manufacturer, has partnered with MINIEYE, a China-based intelligent driving and in-cabin solutions provider listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, to accelerate the deployment of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems and Driver Monitoring Systems tailored specifically for the Indian automotive market. The partnership is focused on adapting intelligent driving technologies to India’s unique and highly complex road environment. As part of the collaboration, Sterling Tools will support perception tuning and on-ground industry engagement, enabling ADAS and driver monitoring systems to be trained for India-specific road scenarios, mixed traffic conditions, and diverse driving patterns. This approach recognises that intelligent driving systems require deep data-driven perception development and application-level engineering to operate reliably in Indian conditions, rather than being direct replications of solutions deployed in global markets. chunks.title: stradvision-india-cv
chunks.text: Accessibility Statement Skip Navigation SEOUL, South Korea, April 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- STRADVISION, a company specializing in AI-based vision perception technology for automotive applications, today announced that a global commercial vehicle OEM has selected SVNet for deployment across its India vehicle lineup. The program targets fleet-scale ADAS deployment in India's commercial vehicle segment, where cost-efficient and reliable perception software is critical to broad adoption. India's commercial vehicle market presents a distinct set of requirements for ADAS deployment. Delivering reliable perception at scale requires software capable of running on low-cost, resource-constrained hardware while maintaining stable performance across diverse and high-density traffic conditions. For commercial vehicle operators, where uptime and operating efficiency are central concerns, both technical performance and deployment economics must be addressed. SVNet is designed to meet these requirements. chunks.title: Why this memo exists
chunks.text: The GTM playbook's spine is Act 5: protected PSU revenue funds the tapeout. Five independent advisors computed the same arithmetic and none of them could make it work. Until this decision is closed, the capacity split, the funding sequence, the Tier-1 motion and the framing of the ASIC are all downstream of an unanswered question — and none of them can be corrected. The tapeout is currently treated as a fixed input to the plan. It is the largest open variable in it.

chunks.title: The two branches, stated plainly
chunks.text: If Column B is viable: there is no Rs 20–35 Cr hole. Act 5 evaporates. PSU revenue becomes profit rather than a mortgage payment. Decisions (a) and (c) both need rewriting, and the company's identity shifts from "we own the die" to "we own India-tuned perception." That is a smaller story and a much shorter path to certified revenue. If Column B is not viable: the honest ICP for the next twelve months is a lead investor plus one NRE-funding Tier-1 partner. The sales organisation's job for that period is generating design-in evidence that closes the round — not booking PSU kit revenue. The playbook must be rewritten around that, and the 50/30/20 split is wrong as drawn. Both branches change the deck fundamentally. Neither is what the current 55 slides say.

chunks.title: Kill-criteria for the tapeout itself
chunks.text: The playbook contains four hard disqualifiers for customer deals and zero for the company's own Rs 25 Cr bet. That asymmetry is not serious. Adopt these, or write better ones: 1. Funding. If committed funding (equity + non-dilutive + Tier-1 NRE) has not reached the quoted tapeout cost by the tapeout decision date, do not tape out. 2. Anchor design-in. If no Tier-1 or OEM has signed an evaluation agreement naming the part before tapeout, the die ships into a market with no committed buyer. 3. Certification path. If AEC-Q100 and an ISO 26262 safety plan are not funded and scheduled, H1 2028 silicon cannot be line-fitted and the margin case cannot be realised. 4. Merchant-SoC parity. If a quoted merchant part reaches a 2027 ship date with qualification in hand and within an agreed cost delta of our die, the die is a luxury.

Bringing together global expertise and local validation, ZF delivers ADAS solutions that meet stringent regulations and future automation needs. With its globally proven reliability, inclusive design and a commitment to safer roads, ZF is driving India toward smarter, safer and sustainable transportation - Redefining India’s Mobility. chunks.title: About ZF
chunks.text: ZF is a global technology company supplying advanced mobility products and systems for passenger cars, commercial vehicles and industrial technology. Its comprehensive product range is primarily aimed at vehicle manufacturers, mobility providers and start-up companies in the fields of transportation and mobility. ZF electrifies a wide range of vehicle types. With its products, the company contributes to reducing emissions, protecting the climate as well as enhancing safe mobility. Alongside the automotive sector – passenger cars and commercial vehicles – ZF also serves market segments such as construction and agricultural machinery, wind power, marine propulsion, rail drives and test systems. With some 161,600 employees worldwide, ZF reported sales of €41.4 billion in fiscal 2024. The company operates 161 production locations in 30 countries. For further press information and photos, please visit: www.zf.com

chunks.title: About CVS Division
chunks.text: ZF’s Commercial Vehicle Solutions (CVS) division is shaping the future of commercial transportation ecosystems. ZF’s CVS division makes commercial vehicles safer, smarter and sustainable to achieve the vision of zero accidents and zero emissions. With its comprehensive technology portfolio, ZF CVS offers tailored solutions for every step of an OEM and fleets’ transformation journey, helping solve complex problems while creating long term value. ZF CVS’s unique capability to digitalize commercial vehicle systems solutions and enhance vehicle intelligence is paving the way towards the commercial vehicle of the future. ZF CVS unites ZF’s former Commercial Vehicle Technology and Commercial Vehicle Control Systems divisions, the latter being formed following ZF’s acquisition of WABCO in Spring 2020. What the raise funds. One-time NRE turns into a chip that costs ~$3 at volume vs $3,000-8,000 incumbents. Blue = input, black = formula.

D. SoC4 5nm SLIP SENSITIVITY
Silicon & Compute revenue FY32 (on-time) — 194.3
Haircut if SoC4 tapes out 12 months late — 0.3
Silicon & Compute revenue FY32 (slip case) — 136.01; ~Rs58 Cr lost; chip+box ramp pushed one year right
If SoC4 5nm slips 12 months, FY32 Silicon & Compute revenue falls ~30% (~Rs58 Cr). Core road-ADAS business on SoC2 is unaffected.
E. BEYOND FY32 — THE NEXT GROWTH WAVE
SoC4 5nm is the option on the next two markets, both arriving post-FY32:
1. Robotaxi / L4 on Indian roads — SoC4 is the compute to win it; we are chip-ready when the market arrives.
2. Datacenter-class chipset — a bigger bet: the same transformer-native architecture scaled to datacenter inference.
The Rs300 Cr cumulative R&D (FY28-32) is not a cost centre — it funds these two options from operating profit, so the
FY33+ growth wave needs no new external capital for silicon. This is why R&D runs high by design.

chunks.title: Tapeout Expenses · Business Plan v2 (part 3)
chunks.text:
SoC4 5nm is the option on the next two markets, both arriving post-FY32:
1. Robotaxi / L4 on Indian roads — SoC4 is the compute to win it; the company are chip-ready when the market arrives.
2. Datacenter-class chipset — a bigger bet: the same transformer-native architecture scaled to datacenter inference.
The Rs300 Cr cumulative R&D (FY28-32) is not a cost centre — it funds these two options from operating profit, so the
FY33+ growth wave needs no new external capital for silicon. This is why R&D runs high by design.

A flat 8×8 matrix unit (SoC1.2) needs 8 cycles to consume K. The 8×8×8 cube (SoC2) consumes K in one cycle by stacking 8 multiply layers — same answer, different geometry. DGrid's batch dispatch firmware (Patent 1) decouples inference execution from RISC-V host supervision — ALU is active 200× longer per cycle. Same real-world fps as a 200+ TOPS system, at 68.7 effective TOPS on a 42mm² die (TSMC 28nm, $630K NRE) vs 7nm tapeout at $15M+. RISC-V host decoupled from ALU. Co-designing the firmware and hardware architecture took 18 months of FPGA iteration — cannot be replicated from a spec sheet. 6-Chiplet Combo Die 64 PCOREs × 512 MACs = 32,768 MACs on ~57.1mm². Replicating this requires 6 separate tapeouts at ~$15M+ total NRE — plus six qualification cycles. 12-Bit Native Radar ADC — The Asymmetric Safety Advantage 12-Bit Native Radar Every competitor (TI AWR2944, NXP S32R) re-quantises radar ADC output to INT16, discarding 4 bits of dynamic range. R100’s 12-bit native radar ADC delivers 4× better target detection sensitivity in low-SNR conditions (monsoon, fog) by preserving full dynamic range. Patent 9 — full radar dynamic range preserved.

chunks.text: 1 Executive summary Revision note. This version incorporates a second adversarial review focused on distribution. Net effect: the addressable market is narrowed to the organised segment (§3) because 75–80% of Indian operators own fewer than five trucks SOURCED ; a channel architecture and a stripped compliance SKU are added (§6); the low-end competitor at ₹4,500–11,000 is named in §7; ASP erosion is flagged against the flat-price assumption in §8; and two risks (11, 12) are added. The FY32 trajectory is unchanged as a target, but it now depends explicitly on OEM line-fit and channel rather than on direct sales into the 5M base. This is the India plan, and it is the funded one. A companion document, BP-1B, covers United States market entry — a different buyer, a different trigger and a different product posture, owned by an incoming co-founder and carrying no revenue forecast. Nothing in this document depends on that one. This document contains two plans, not one. Part A is India: funded, dated, and driven by a compliance mandate. Part B is the United States: a different buyer, a different trigger and a different product posture, owned by an incoming co-founder and deliberately carrying no revenue forecast until a first partner conversation closes. Part C is what they share — one raise, one tapeout, one risk register. Revision note.

chunks.text: Executive summary. DeepGrid Semi sells the certification stamp, not the autonomy dream. MoRTH GSR 184(E), live April 2026, mandates certified ADAS on every new N2/N3 commercial truck sold in India — a regulatory demand floor across a 5M+ truck base. The AD2 kit prices at ₹2.3L (₹2–2.5L band) PLAN against imports at ₹6.5L (Mobileye EyeQ6) to ₹15L (Nvidia Orin) — a ~2.8–6.5× gap ASSUMPTION ARITHMETIC PLAN . Owning the compute (28nm die, packaged part ₹1,750 ) lets us hold that price while gross margin expands from 45% (FPGA phase, FY27) to ~72% in the ASIC phase. Three stacked motions run on one hardware platform: (1) fleet retrofit kits now — no regulatory gate, revenue from day one; (2) OEM/Tier-1 line-fit for the mandate channel — the volume engine, entered after AIS-162/188 certification; (3) privateland driverless at ports, mines and plant yards — sold as per-vehicle-per-month software at 90%+ gross margin. The first retrofit customers are plant operators with private yards: one logo carries the kit sale, the data flywheel, and the future driverless contract. Primary planning numbers, from the working model (Business Plan v2.2): ADAS segment revenue ₹914 Cr at FY32 inside a company total of ₹1,388 Cr, with EBITDA breakeven in FY2028. Traction today: ₹1.01 Cr defence revenue CONTRACTED MEASURED ; AD0-class perception proven on FPGA (40 fps YOLOv11n ).

OEM/Tier-1 design-in is relationship-gated: comparable regulation-created hardware markets (EU tachograph, eCall) show mandate volume normally flows to whichever supplier already has OEM relationships and homologation experience, not the cheapest new entrant — those incumbents typically absorbed aftermarket share within ~18 months once line-fit normalized EXTERNAL REFERENCE . This plan therefore pursues OEM/Tier-1 engagement opportunistically from month one (a) AIS-162/188 certification (T2-funded, §9) PLAN , (b) retrofit field- hours and Indian-road data as validation, (c) the T2 milestone clock (§9) — but does not treat a signed design-in as a required, dated event the way §8's revenue trajectory implicitly assumes. The pitch leads with capability, not price: owning perception + compute + model on Jiyu's <100 ms ASIL-D EHB lets us certify a single photon-to-brake latency number no mix-and-match integration can produce — but that pitch needs an actual OEM contact, which this plan does not yet have (§10 risk 10).

chunks.title: Fast case vs. slow case. The plan as financially modeled (§8) is a fast case: …
chunks.text: Fast case vs. slow case. The plan as financially modeled (§8) is a fast case: certification, tapeout and first OEM engagement all land inside 12–18 months. Comparable mandatedriven hardware markets have historically taken 3–5 years to move from mandate announcement to stable incumbent share EXTERNAL REFERENCE . In the slow case, FY27– FY29 revenue rests almost entirely on government/defence and insurer-co-funded retrofit (this section) while certification and OEM engagement continue in the background with no committed date — the fast case is upside, not the base the company should be funded against. The three phases are the spine of this plan, so they are set out as a matrix rather than described in prose. Read Figure 8 as the answer to four questions per phase: who we sell to, through whom, at what price, and what has to be true before the next phase opens.

chunks.title: The uncomfortable reading, kept in deliberately. Against imports we are three times …
chunks.text: The uncomfortable reading, kept in deliberately. Against imports we are three times cheaper. Against the device that actually wins mandated volume in India we are twenty times more expensive. Both statements are true, and a serious investor will find the second one. Our answer has to be that we are not selling into the same job: a ₹5,000 box satisfies an inspector, while our kit is what an OEM can put on a production line and a fleet can build a safety case on. That answer only holds if (a) enforcement eventually becomes real, (b) we win OEM line-fit, and (c) we field a stripped SKU for the segment that only wants compliance (§6). If none of those three lands, the low end takes the mandate and we are left with the organised segment alone. Moat, in order of durability: 1. Structural price floor: owned silicon at <$3–4/bare die (₹1,750 packaged, §5) makes the ₹2.3L price ours to hold; importers cannot follow down without destroying their own margin stack. 2. Certification + sovereignty: claimed only-indigenous AIS-validated chipset, AIS-004 native, 15 patents filed; foreign silicon excluded from government/defence fleets (§2). Certification is a path, not held — the killer risk, §10. 3. Data moat that compounds — narrower than it sounds.

chunks.title: Three things this changes. EBITDA breakeven is FY2028 at +₹2.59 Cr, and net income turns …
chunks.text: Three things this changes. EBITDA breakeven is FY2028 at +₹2.59 Cr, and net income turns positive in FY2029 at +₹19.85 Cr — the plan reaches profitability one year after the raise, not at some unstated future point. Gross margin runs 53.4% → 88.4%, so the 88% figure is the model’s planned blended margin rather than an aspiration, though it remains a blend and not a kit-level number (§5). And FY32 EBITDA margin is 38.7%, not the 43% quoted in the June 2026 Information Memorandum — the lower figure is the one to use. The assumption the model rests on, unchanged from the earlier warning. Every ASP in the Revenue Master is held flat from FY27 to FY32 — the truck kit at ₹2.50L, the smart mirror at ₹0.50L, the dies at their launch prices. Indian mandate-created hardware markets have historically eroded ASP faster than COGS (§7). A Series-A model needs an erosion case: at 8–12% annual ASP decline from FY29 ASSUMPTION the FY32 ADAS line would fall materially below ₹914 Cr even with volumes held. That sensitivity is the single most valuable thing to add to v2.2 before this goes to an institutional investor.

Share buyback or The clawback we were relying on as the transfer at a pre-agreed price runs into FEMA transfer-pricing enforcement lever is the weakest part of the old constraints structure, not the strongest What replaces the tranche gate. The instrument is CCPS with a milestone-linked conversion ratio. The investor funds $1M now and is fully invested; how many equity shares the CCPS converts into flexes with the agreed growth milestones. CCPS expressly support performance-linked milestones and valuation-linked conversion ratios SOURCED , and because the money is received at a single certified price, the FEMA problem above never arises. Economically it delivers what the clawback was meant to deliver — fewer shares on conversion is the same thing as a higher effective entry price — but it is executable, which the clawback may not be. Two things we accept in exchange, and should say plainly rather than discover later: the company gives up the discipline of withheld cash, and a conversion-ratio adjustment is contested at conversion rather than settled by simply not wiring money ASSUMPTION .

chunks.text: Shravan, You have offered to come in as an investor, and separately you have said you would like to come in as a co-founder and bring your experience taking businesses international. I want to take the second offer more seriously than the first, because I think it is worth more to this company than the cheque — and because it deserves a real answer rather than an enthusiastic one. So I have written you a document about America specifically, kept apart from our India plan. I did that deliberately. Our India story is genuinely strong, and if I had merged the two you would have found the Indian tailwind quietly carrying the American argument. You would have discovered that yourself in month four, and you would have been right to be annoyed about it. What follows is what I actually believe, including the parts that make our US position look smaller than a founder normally admits in writing. Where a number is from our own material I have said so; where it is from outside research I have cited it. Everything I have not verified is marked as an assumption. I would rather you enter this knowing exactly what is unproven than have you find out after you have put your name on it. There is one thing I want to say plainly at the start. I take delivery — the silicon, the certification, the engineering. I am proposing that you take the market, starting with America.

chunks.text: Why that fourth column changes the plan. S1, S2 and S6 carry no longevity gate and no automotive silicon qualification at all — nobody demands a fifteen-year supply commitment on a soft-IP licence, a software model, or a private-land stack. S4, the packaged chip, is the biggest prize and the one thing we genuinely cannot sell into automotive yet. So the ladder is S2 and S6 first, S1 and S3 next, S4 last, and the honest conclusion is that our first American revenue is far more likely to be a licence than a part. I want to flag what that implies about the job, because it affects whether this partnership is the right fit rather than just an attractive one. Selling soft IP or a perception model to a Tier-1 is a long-cycle, technical, relationship-led enterprise sale — much closer to licensing than to distribution. If that is the kind of selling you have done, this works. If your strength is channel and volume distribution, then S6 — yard autonomy — is where you should start, and we should both know that going in. 6 What it costs to play in this category I would rather show you this than have you discover it.

chunks.text: I agree with it, I think it is better than anything I had written, and it fixes the one real hole in this document: everything up to §9 ends at “gated on Series A” with no American capital plan at all. So here is that plan, with the parts I would push back on marked as such. Why the reference asset changes our position Today I walk into an American conversation with measured silicon and a good story. In 2028, if India goes the way BP-1A says it should, I walk in with something categorically different — a deployed fleet, field-failure data from a punishing duty cycle, and manufacturing maturity somebody else has already paid to prove. No amount of pitching substitutes for that, and it is the one asset the companies in §7 cannot simply buy with funding. But I want to be precise about what it proves, because overselling this is how the document would lose its credibility: THE INDIA FLEET PROVES IT DOES NOT PROVE Reliability at a hostile duty cycle — heat, vibration, dust, US regulatory compliance. AIS certification is not voltage transients, tamper resistance over real months FMVSS, and the test protocols differ Manufacturing and field maturity — that we can build, US highway perception validation. Indian road data install, support and service at volume does not validate American interstate conditions Unit economics at real volume — our cost floor Automotive qualification.

That means the same OEM is simultaneously an ADAS customer and a yard-autonomy platform partner — our S3 module and our S6 stack sold to one buyer, on one relationship, through one integration. Every other route in §4 needs a different partner for each product. This one does not, which makes the smaller-OEM segment our best single target rather than merely the easiest one. Your point also forces a correction on my own SKU logic. In §5 I argued the licence SKUs come first because they dodge the longevity gate. That holds for Tier-1s and autonomy companies, who have their own engineering teams. Smaller OEMs are the opposite: they lack integration capacity, so they want a more complete product, not bare RTL.

Three Industries. Deepgrid Semi is an autonomous systems company from Hyderabad. We design a single indigenous chip — DGrid Alpha — and point it at three industries at once: vehicle safety on India's roads, defence robotics and drones, and the industrial silicon India imports today. One design investment, three revenue engines, zero import dependence. chunks.title: S T R I C T LY C O N F I D E N T I A L · F O R A U T H O R I S E D R E C I P I E N T S O … (cont.)
chunks.text: The same silicon powers ADAS, Defence and Industrial products, and one Sentience AI layer learns across all three — delivering safer roads, indigenous chips, and low-cost chips. Cost figures are engineering estimates. T H E T H R E E I N D U S T R I E S — O N E S I L I C O N C O R E U N D E R N E AT H ADAS — Vehicle Safety Defence — Robots & Drones India's roads are the world's deadliest, and the government has now made driver-assistance mandatory on commercial trucks — covering the national fleet. Imported kits are priced out of reach; ours is not, because we own the chip inside it. The Indian Army is already our paying customer, with hardware fielded and reviewed by senior command. The same die carries a military-grade chiplet — and India's first indigenous drone flightcontrol, navigation and AI chip. Industrial — Warehouse & Indoor Autonomy UGVs, AMRs and inventory drones for warehouses, factories and campuses — GPS never works indoors, and our autonomy stack was built for exactly that. A working load-carrying platform has already been demonstrated. How to read this document: the ADAS story follows next, then the investment in DGrid Alpha, then the Defence and Industrial pages — where we talk numbers. The final page is the long-horizon compute roadmap. That is the whole story in one picture. It begins where the pain is worst — on India's roads.

chunks.title: S T R I C T LY C O N F I D E N T I A L · F O R A U T H O R I S E D R E C I P I E N T S O …
chunks.text: S T R I C T LY C O N F I D E N T I A L · F O R A U T H O R I S E D R E C I P I E N T S O N LY INDUSTRY 2 O F 3 — DEFENCE · RO B O TS & DRO NES D E F E NCE · D 1 0 0 The Army Already Pays Us — And the Drone Chip Rides the Same Die Defence is not a promise on a slide: ₹1.01 Cr is contracted via MCEME / Indian Army, with hardware fielded and reviewed by senior command. The D100 chiplet turns the same DGrid Alpha tapeout into military-grade compute — lockstep RISC-V safety cores (ASIL-D path), AES-256 secure enclave — at zero additional design cost. W HY F LIG HT CONT ROL + V IO + AI MUS T LIV E ON ONE CHIP FC — Fly VIO — Know Where You Are AI — See & Decide The flight-control loop keeps the drone in the air — real-time, deterministic, every millisecond. It cannot wait on another chip. GPS is jammed along the LoC/LAC and never works indoors. Visual-inertial navigation is the only positioning that survives — geometry, not GPS. Onboard detection and obstacle avoidance when the comms link is gone — the drone must think for itself, on the drone. Fused on one die, they become a hardware fail-safe: when the link or GPS fails, the FC loop reads VIO position directly — same silicon, same clock, no bus, no second board — and flies itself home. Split across chips, that path gains latency, weight, power and failure points; a drone falling over a city or into stacked inventory is a lawsuit.

chunks.title: Executive Summary: The Pre-Series A Strategic Crossroads
chunks.text: The commercial autonomous vehicle (AV) and advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) semiconductor market is characterized by structural capital intensity, prolonged design-in validation cycles, and significant cash burn before achieving commercial viability1. Within this high-barrier landscape, DeepGrid Semi, currently incubated at T-Hub Phase 2 in Hyderabad, stands at a critical technological and commercial crossroads1. As an early-stage, pre-revenue fabless semiconductor startup, DeepGrid has successfully validated its custom INT8 edge-AI architecture on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs)1. However, the enterprise currently lacks established Tier-1 automotive customers or the massive capital required to transition from high-cost FPGA prototyping—which currently costs approximately () per board—to mass-produced custom Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), projected to cost less than () per chip at scale1. To fund the physical fabrication of its custom combo-die, DeepGrid is actively seeking to raise a () Pre-Series A venture capital round1. For institutional investors, technical validation on FPGAs is insufficient; the primary investment thesis depends on demonstrating a realistic, rapid path to commercial traction and cash-flow generation1.

chunks.title: Executive Summary: The Pre-Series A Strategic Crossroads
chunks.text: This report establishes a systematic framework for identifying DeepGrid’s Ideal Customer Profiles (ICPs) and maps out actionable Go-To-Market (GTM) strategies customized to these profiles1. By analyzing the commercial playbooks of global autonomous vehicle leaders and domestic Indian semiconductor startups, this report outlines how DeepGrid can leverage near-term regulatory safety mandates, dual-use tactical contracts, and unique hardware price advantages to bypass traditional multi-year automotive OEM cycles, mitigate capital burn, and build a highly defensible, localized data moat in India and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) markets1.

source.label: ICP and GTM Strategy (Jul 2026) · Executive Summary: The Pre-Series A Strategic Crossroads

chunks.title: Systematic Methodology for Identifying DeepGrid’s ICP
chunks.text: A common point of failure for fabless semiconductor startups is targeting broad, unconstrained market segments without evaluating customer buying behaviors, technical integration friction, and regulatory timelines1. To optimize its limited Pre-Series A capital, DeepGrid must utilize a rigorous, multi-dimensional diagnostic framework to identify, score, and prioritize potential customer segments1. The systematic methodology relies on five critical strategic evaluation dimensions: Regulatory Compulsion Index: This dimension measures whether the customer's purchase is discretionary or driven by immediate, non-discretionary legislative mandates1. Segments facing hard regulatory compliance deadlines (such as India's upcoming heavy vehicle safety standards or Saudi Arabia's tracking laws) are prioritized because they exhibit condensed sales cycles and low marketing friction4. Technical Integration & Certification Friction: This parameter evaluates the engineering hours, architectural modifications, and safety homologation testing (such as ISO 26262 functional safety, AIS-004 electromagnetic compatibility, and AIS-189 cybersecurity certifications) required to design DeepGrid's silicon into the customer's platform7. Higher integration complexity delays time-to-revenue and increases cash burn1.

source.label: ICP and GTM Strategy (Jul 2026) · Systematic Methodology for Identifying DeepGrid’s ICP

chunks.title: Systematic Methodology for Identifying DeepGrid’s ICP
chunks.text: Price Elasticity & BOM Limit: This dimension analyzes the customer's tolerance for hardware acquisition costs1. Large commercial transport fleets and logistics networks in emerging markets exhibit extreme price sensitivity and thin operational margins, making them highly receptive to DeepGrid's projected low-cost ASIC board Bill of Materials (BOM) of , compared to expensive foreign imported computing systems costing upwards of 1. Sales Cycle & Time-to-Revenue Duration: This metric measures the duration between initial technical engagement and commercial volume shipments1. Direct passenger vehicle OEM sales cycles typically span three to five years, whereas off-highway industrial projects or defense research contracts often finalize procurement in under six to twelve months1. Operational Design Domain (ODD) Entropy: This dimension maps the physical environments of the application, contrasting highly structured, predictable interstate highways with unstructured, chaotic urban roadways and off-highway terrains1. High-entropy environments require real-world, localized training datasets that can process unique local variables (such as three-wheelers, unlit vehicles, and wandering livestock), which provides a natural moat against general-purpose global computing platforms1.

chunks.text: Option A targets tactical military unmanned systems, national security agencies, and heavy off-highway industrial operators, such as seaports, mining terminals, and enclosed manufacturing campuses1. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ ICP OPTION A: TACTICAL DEFENSE & OFF-HIGHWAY │ ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ • Targets: Unmanned Ground Vehicles, Port AGVs, Campus AMRs. │ │ • Primary Pain Point: Lack of secure, localized, low-latency compute.│ │ • Key Silicon Enabler: D100 lockstep secure RISC-V enclave. │ │ • Buying Behavior: Insensitive to cost; demands high IP sovereignty.│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ The underlying buying behavior in this segment is driven by a critical need for secure, localized computing hardware that operates reliably in high-entropy, GPS-denied environments without relying on external cloud communications1. National defense agencies require absolute intellectual property sovereignty and hardware-level cybersecurity to prevent external jamming or unauthorized system overrides1.

chunks.title: Option A: Tactical Defense and Constrained Off-Highway Environments
chunks.text: In this context, DeepGrid's inclusion of the D100 lockstep secure RISC-V enclave directly addresses these national defense specifications, providing an isolated cryptographic execution environment for tactical Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) and automated logistical systems1. This buying profile is highly insensitive to upfront hardware costs but demands military-grade physical system hardening, wide thermal operating tolerances, and direct access to raw sensory processing engines1. In the industrial off-highway sub-segment, such as automated guided vehicles (AGVs) operating in major commercial seaports, the customer's pain point is operational efficiency and collision mitigation within tightly constrained spatial zones1. This profile is highly receptive to the direct integration of the R100 radar DSP and the T100 thermal/LiDAR DSP on a single silicon die, which eliminates the latency and physical reliability issues associated with multi-chip board configurations on heavy industrial machinery1.

chunks.title: Option C: Sovereign Compliance and OEM Factory Line-Fit Embedding
chunks.text: Integrating a suite of mandatory safety systems—including advanced emergency braking, blind spot monitoring, lane departure warnings, and driver drowsiness alerts—typically requires mounting multiple separate electronic control units (ECUs), sensor processors, and CAN gateways from different Tier-1 suppliers, which inflates the vehicle's manufacturing BOM and creates complex software integration bottlenecks1. OEM buyers are highly receptive to DeepGrid's single-die, six-chiplet system-on-chip architecture, which consolidates AI processing (A100), radar DSP (R100), secure computing (D100), and vehicle gateway telematics (S100) onto a single silicon substrate1. This level of integration eliminates multi-chip board complexity, reduces the physical footprint within the vehicle's electrical cabinet, and lowers the vehicle's platform manufacturing cost1. However, because these buyers will not purchase directly from an unproven, pre-revenue startup, they require DeepGrid to integrate with their preferred, established Tier-1 automotive component suppliers1. These Tier-1 channel partners act as the interface, absorbing physical assembly, long-term product warranties, and vehicle integration liabilities1.

By integrating the lockstep RISC-V secure enclave (D100) directly on the FPGA board, DeepGrid can bid on sovereign-compliance research and development contracts1. DeepGrid can leverage this to offset EDA tool licensing costs and foundry multi-project wafer (MPW) fabrication fees39. Deployment Linked Incentive: Provides financial incentives ranging from to of net sales turnover over five years, capped at per application, directly subsidizing DeepGrid's volume scaling phase39. An MPW shuttle run shares mask-set costs across multiple startup designs on a single reticle, reducing the entry cost of first-silicon to approximately to for a typical to die area47. Early retrofit units can run on optimized FPGA architectures, transitioning seamlessly to the custom ASIC once first-silicon is verified and delivered1. The target segment is private and truck fleets that must comply with the impending regulatory deadlines1. By pricing its hardware kit at to (representing a massive discount compared to premium imported systems costing upwards of ), DeepGrid can drive rapid, high-volume aftermarket retrofits across thousands of active fleet vehicles1.

chunks.title: Custom Silicon Cost Advantage vs. Foreign Competitors
chunks.text: The primary driver of DeepGrid's economic advantage is its complete vertical integration1. Western autonomous computing platforms rely on general-purpose GPUs and CPUs, which require highly complex, multi-chip board configurations featuring separate processors, radar DSPs, CAN controllers, and secure enclaves1. This design drives their compute board BOM to over , forcing these incumbents to target premium, high-margin logistics networks in developed markets to justify the high capital expenditure1. DeepGrid's custom system-on-chip design integrates six functional chiplets—including AI acceleration (A100), radar DSP (R100), secure RISC-V compute (D100), and a vehicle telematics gateway (S100)—directly onto a single silicon substrate1. chunks.title: Actionable Recommendations: The Pre-Series A VC Investment Thesis
chunks.text: For venture capitalists evaluating DeepGrid Semi against global autonomy platforms and domestic semiconductor design startups, the investment thesis is built on three core strategic pillars1: Eliminating the "Hardware Squeeze Zone" via Vertical Integration: Software-only autonomous vehicle startups are structurally squeezed by high third-party hardware costs, as they are forced to purchase expensive merchant silicon compute engines to run their algorithms1. By executing complete vertical integration—designing its own ASIC, integrated radar DSP, and physical compute system—DeepGrid avoids this margin squeeze, capturing both premium hardware margins and high-margin recurring SaaS software revenue1. De-Risking Early Cash-Burn via the Dual-Use Tactical Wedge: DeepGrid is not a pre-revenue startup burning cash while waiting for long-horizon passenger vehicle OEM contracts to mature1. By deploying its currently functional FPGA platforms directly into tactical defense projects and port AGV environments, DeepGrid generates immediate, high-margin contract cash-flow1. This dual-use strategy provides vital operational validation data, cushions the startup's burn rate, and builds physical proof-of-concept traction to de-risk the TSMC tape-out phase1.

chunks.title: Actionable Recommendations: The Pre-Series A VC Investment Thesis
chunks.text: Capital Efficiency via Sovereign Compliance and Mature Nodes: While foreign incumbents burn hundreds of millions of dollars attempting to design chips on expensive FinFET nodes1, DeepGrid's utilization of TSMC's mature HPC+ node represents an extremely capital-efficient engineering path1. Supported by the India Semiconductor Mission's Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme—which subsidizes up to of eligible chip design expenditure and offers sales-linked incentives39—DeepGrid’s requested Pre-Series A round provides a realistic, fully funded path to first-silicon delivery, system validation, and rapid market deployment1. In summary, DeepGrid's GTM strategy intelligently adapts the dual-use pragmatism of Kodiak and the constrained-environment focus of Gatik to the unique regulatory landscape of India and the GCC1. Funding DeepGrid is a calculated bet that aggressive vertical integration on a mature node is the only economically viable method to capture the impending, mandate-driven commercial vehicle safety and autonomy market1.
